Def: Unconscious child: an airway problem before a neurology problem.
Cause: AEIOU-TIPS is the mnemonic list of causes of coma.
Alcohol, epilepsy, insulin, opiates, uraemia, trauma, infection, psychiatric, shock, space-occupying lesion.
Patho: Structural causes: focal and asymmetric; metabolic/toxic: global and symmetric.
CPP = MAP - ICP; raised ICP → Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing).
Uncal herniation: CN III compression → dilated pupil; tonsillar → cardiopulmonary arrest.
Signs: Opioids: respiratory and CNS depression, pinpoint pupils.
Decorticate: flexed arms; decerebrate: extended arms.
Expose: purpura, odd bruises (abuse), needle marks.
Dx: Never skip a bedside glucose.
Head CT if GCS ≤ 14, skull fracture or focal signs.
Never do a lumbar puncture with raised ICP or shock.
Rx: ABCDE; GCS of 8 or less → intubation; naloxone for pinpoint pupils.
Meningitis possible: ceftriaxone immediately, don't wait for lumbar puncture.
Raised ICP: elevate head, hyperventilate, mannitol.

topics.title: Causes and treatment of convulsion in childhood

Def: Status epilepticus: seizure lasting ≥ 5 min → treat on the 5-5-5 ladder.
Cause: A neonatal seizure is always pathological: HIE, hypoglycaemia, low Ca/Na, sepsis, haemorrhage.
Toddler: febrile seizure commonest (3-5% of children), meningitis, NAI, West syndrome.
Older: epilepsy, trauma, tumour, AVM.
Patho: Excitatory synapses mature before inhibitory ones → low seizure threshold.
Rapid temperature rise or metabolic insult → threshold crossed.
Signs: Absence: blank stare, provoked by hyperventilation.
Focal impaired awareness: staring, head tilting, mouth chewing, confusion.
West syndrome: bilateral jerking, hypsarrhythmia.
Dx: Bedside glucose at 0 min; check Ca, Na; screen for infection.
First seizure: EEG and CT head without contrast (emergency) or MRI.
Rx: 5 min first benzodiazepine; 10 min second benzodiazepine; 15 min levetiracetam, phenytoin or valproate; 25 min RSI.
Neonates: phenobarbital, pyridoxine if resistant; West: ACTH.

Def: Primary (migraine, tension-type - benign) vs secondary headache.
Cause: Primary: migraine and tension-type = overwhelming majority.
Childhood CNS tumors are usually infratentorial: pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, ependymoma.
Also idiopathic intracranial hypertension, medication overuse headache.
Patho: Raised ICP → worse on waking, coughing, lying flat; vomiting without nausea.
Raised ICP → new CN VI palsy = false localising sign.
Signs: Migraine: throbbing, nausea, photophobia; 4 to 72 hours; in children often bilateral, as short as 2 hours.
Tension: bilateral, constant, no aura; chronic = 15 days/month for more than 3 months.
Dx: Three questions: acute or chronic, progressive or not, red flags.
Red flags: awakening from sleep, coordination difficulties, focal signs, age under 5 years.
Any red flag → urgent neuroimaging, preferably MRI.
Rx: Acute migraine: NSAIDs or acetaminophen first-line; also triptans.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: acetazolamide (± furosemide).
Headache diary for triggers; prophylaxis if frequent.

Def: Infant with fever ≥ 38 °C; under 3 months they cannot localise infection.
Cause: Neonatal sepsis: group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria; consider HSV.
Commonest serious bacterial infection: urinary tract infection.
Patho: Immature immunity + no vaccine cover + no localising signs → appearance unreliable.
Signs: Meningitis = poor feeding, 'not right'; no neck stiffness.
Non-blanching rash → meningococcal sepsis; fever >5 days → think Kawasaki.
Dx: Under 28 days: full septic screen incl. lumbar puncture for all.
1-3 months: FBC, CRP, culture, urine; LP if unwell.
Over 3 months: traffic-light system; urine in everyone: clean catch, not a bag.
Rx: Under 28 days: admit + IV ampicillin (amoxicillin) + gentamicin/cefotaxime; ± aciclovir.
Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins; non-blanching rash → antibiotics first.
Well over 3 months with viral source → home with safety-netting.

topics.title: Rash and fever in children (incubation periods as well!)

Def: Fever + rash: first ask does it blanch?, then pattern-match.
Cause: First measles, second scarlet fever, third rubella, fifth parvovirus, sixth roseola.
Chickenpox: varicella-zoster virus (VZV), airborne.
Emergencies: meningococcaemia, Kawasaki, SJS/TEN, toxic shock.
Patho: Non-blanching + fever → meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise.
Petechiae above the nipple line after coughing or vomiting: raised venous pressure.
Chickenpox lesions are in different stages.
Signs: Measles rash starts behind the ears; Koplik spots; death from pneumonia.
Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue; parvovirus: slapped cheek.
Rubella: suboccipital nodes. Coxsackie A: hand, foot and mouth disease.
Dx: Glass test; then morphology, site of onset, timing vs fever.
Incubation: varicella 10-21 days; rubella 14-21 days; measles 10-14 d; scarlet 2-5 d.
Rx: Suspected meningococcal sepsis → benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone immediately.
Severe chickenpox: IV acyclovir; newborn of infected mother: VZIG.
Kawasaki → IVIG within 10 days.

topics.title: Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO) and Kawasaki syndrome

Def: FUO: fever >38 °C ≥ 8 days, no cause after initial evaluation.
Kawasaki: fever ≥ 5 days plus 4 of 5 principal features.
Cause: FUO is most often infection (~50%), then inflammatory disease (~20%), then malignancy (~10%).
Kawasaki classically affects Asian children.
Patho: Kawasaki hits the coronary arteries → aneurysm → rupture or myocardial infarction.
sJIA with falling ESR, cytopenias, high ferritin → macrophage activation syndrome.
Signs: Kawasaki conjunctivitis: bilateral, non-purulent, limbal sparing.
Thrombocytosis in the second week; high CRP/ESR, sterile pyuria.
sJIA: daily spiking fevers, salmon-pink macular rash.
Dx: FUO: repeated daily history and examination is the highest-yield investigation.
Suspected Kawasaki: CRP or ESR; echocardiogram at diagnosis, then 1-2 and 4-6 weeks.
Rx: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin within 10 days; aspirin exception despite Reye syndrome.
No defervescence → second IVIG; refractory → steroids/infliximab.
Incomplete Kawasaki: under 1 year, highest aneurysm risk; delay vaccines 8 months.

topics.title: Differential diagnosis and treatment of neonatal respiratory distress

Def: Newborn with tachypnoea >60, grunting, flaring, recession, cyanosis.
Cause: RDS: prematurity, maternal diabetes, caesarean; TTN: term caesarean; MAS: term and post-term.
Sepsis; cyanotic CHD, diaphragmatic hernia, choanal atresia, TE fistula.
Patho: Prematurity → inadequate surfactant → alveoli fail to open → poor oxygenation.
TTN: delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.
PPHN: pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall; meconium inactivates surfactant.
Signs: TTN: term C-section baby with grunting, settles in 24-72 hours.
CDH: scaphoid abdomen; choanal atresia: pink when crying.
TE fistula: coughing, choking, cyanosis.
Dx: RDS CXR: ground-glass with air bronchograms; lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio ≥ 2.
No response to 100% oxygen → duct-dependent CHD; PPHN: echocardiography.
NG tube coiling in esophagus → esophageal atresia.
Rx: CPAP for all; RDS: maternal antenatal glucocorticoids, surfactant when FiO₂ exceeds 0.30.
CDH: never bag-mask; intubate with NG tube on suction.
Sepsis: ampicillin + gentamicin (cefotaxime if meningitis); PPHN: nitric oxide.

Def: Classify by onset and conjugated vs unconjugated; UGT conjugates bilirubin.
Cause: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological: Rh/ABO, G6PD, spherocytosis, sepsis.
Breast milk (β-glucuronidase); Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar: unconjugated.
Conjugated: biliary atresia, hepatitis, choledochal cyst, TORCH, galactosaemia.
Patho: Phototherapy makes bilirubin water-soluble, excreted without hepatic conjugation.
High unconjugated bilirubin → kernicterus.
Rh disease: Rh- mother, Rh+ fetus; not the first pregnancy.
Signs: Prolonged jaundice beyond 2 weeks with pale stools and dark urine = biliary atresia.
Cephalohematoma is subperiosteal, does not cross sutures; encephalopathy: high-pitched cry, opisthotonus.
Dx: Early work-up: blood group, direct Coombs, FBC, film.
Split the bilirubin: conjugated is >25 μmol/L or >20% of total.
Rx: Phototherapy above the line; exchange transfusion if it fails or encephalopathy.
Breastfeeding jaundice: increase feeds; breast milk jaundice: continue breastfeeding.
Anti-D at 28-32 weeks and within 72 hours; Kasai before 60 days.

Def: Central cyanosis (lips, mucous membranes) = low arterial oxygen saturation.
Cause: Respiratory, cardiac, PPHN (SSRIs in pregnancy), methaemoglobinaemia, polycythemia (hematocrit >65%).
Five Ts: truncus, transposition (day 1), tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallot (commonest overall), total anomalous pulmonary venous return.
Patho: PPHN: pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall → right-to-left shunt at PDA and foramen ovale.
Duct closes day 2-3 → collapse.
Signs: Comfortably blue = cardiac, as respiratory drive responds mainly to CO₂; distressed and blue = pulmonary.
Methaemoglobinaemia: chocolate-brown blood, normal PaO₂.
Dx: Hyperoxia test: pulmonary cyanosis improves on 100% O₂; cardiac and PPHN do not.
Pre-ductal saturation on the right hand; difference over 10% suggests PPHN.
Echocardiography is the key investigation.
Rx: Duct-dependent lesions: prostaglandin E1, avoiding excess oxygen.
Transposition: balloon atrial septostomy before arterial switch.
PPHN: inhaled nitric oxide (cGMP); refractory → ECMO; methaemoglobinaemia: methylene blue.

Def: Neonatal hypoglycaemia: blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L.
HHS: glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolarity >320.
Cause: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood is commonest at 1-5 y; GSD, GH/cortisol deficiency.
No ketones → hyperinsulinism (infant of diabetic mother) or fat-oxidation defect (MCAD).
Hyperglycaemia → almost always type 1 DM.
Patho: Maternal diabetes → fetal hyperinsulinism → neonatal hypoglycaemia, macrosomia.
DKA insulin bolus → rapid osmotic shifts → cerebral oedema.
Signs: Autonomic (sweating, tremor, tachycardia, hunger) → neuroglycopenic (confusion, seizures, coma).
Dx: Take the critical sample (insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, GH, ketones) before giving glucose.
Best discriminator: the ketone level at the time of the low sugar.
DKA = glucose + ketosis + pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.
Rx: 2 ml/kg of 10% dextrose, then infusion; glucagon if no access.
Diazoxide for hyperinsulinism; cornstarch (GSD); avoid fasting (MCAD).
DKA: fluids first, then insulin 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h an hour later, no bolus.

Def: Reactive nodes (soft, tender, <2 cm, resolve 4-6 wk) vs malignant nodes.
Cause: Localised: Staphylococcus aureus > Streptococcus pyogenes, cat scratch (Bartonella), atypical mycobacteria, TB.
Generalised: EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HIV, Kawasaki, JIA, SLE, leukaemia, lymphoma.
Patho: EBV: T-cell hyperplasia in the node paracortex.
Staph/Strep lymphadenitis → suppuration, abscess, fluctuance.
Lymphoma diagnosis depends on nodal architecture; mediastinal mass threatens airway.
Signs: EBV: fatigue, fever, posterior cervical nodes, pharyngitis, hepatosplenomegaly.
Worrying: over 2 cm and growing, beyond 6 weeks, supraclavicular, painless.
Cold, violaceous, non-tender node in a toddler: atypical mycobacteria.
Dx: Highest-yield first test: full blood count and film; CRP, LDH, urate, EBV/CMV serology.
Chest X-ray before biopsy to look for a mediastinal mass.
Rx: Soft, mobile, non-tender nodes: observation; reactive nodes resolve in 4-6 weeks.
Suspected lymphoma: excisional biopsy, not FNA.

Def: Joint pain: exclude septic arthritis first, then classify by cause and timing.
Cause: Reactive: rheumatic fever (GAS M protein mimicry); inflammatory: JIA, SLE, HSP; malignant: leukaemia.
Mechanical by age: DDH infancy, Perthes (4-8 years), SUFE obese adolescent.
Septic: Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella osteomyelitis in sickle cell.
Patho: Osteomyelitis starts in the metaphysis (slow-flowing hairpin capillary loops).
Signs: Septic: febrile, toxic, refuses to weight-bear; transient synovitis: afebrile, well, limps.
Morning = inflammatory, after activity = mechanical, night = malignant.
Jones: carditis, polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum; sJIA: quotidian fever.
Dx: Kocher: non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5, ESR >40, WBC >12.
Urgent aspiration + blood cultures; MRI for osteomyelitis.
JIA: onset before 16, lasting at least 6 weeks.
Rx: Aspirate the joint before antibiotics → IV antibiotics + surgical washout.
Transient synovitis: rest and NSAIDs; JIA: methotrexate weekly.
Rheumatic fever: penicillin prophylaxis; macrolides if anaphylaxis.

topics.title: Causes and differential diagnosis of bloody stool in children

Def: Bloody stool: digital rectal examination and haemodynamics first, then narrow by age and story.
Cause: Neonate: swallowed maternal blood, NEC, CMPA, volvulus, vitamin K deficiency.
Toddler: fissure (commonest), intussusception, Meckel's, polyp.
Older: infectious colitis, IBD, HSP, HUS.
Patho: Meckel's bleeds because it contains ectopic gastric mucosa.
Rule of 2s: 2% of people, 2 feet from ileocaecal valve, 2 inches, under age 2.
E. coli O157 toxin → HUS; antibiotics increase toxin release.
Signs: Painful, paroxysmal + sausage mass (3 mo-3 y) → intussusception.
Painless, transfusion-requiring bleeding without diarrhoea → Meckel's.
Bilious vomiting + blood → volvulus.
Dx: Apt test for maternal blood.
Meckel's → technetium-99m pertechnetate scan; intussusception → ultrasound target sign.
HUS: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.
Rx: Shocked → resuscitate first: wide-bore access, fluids, cross-match.
Intussusception: enema reduction. Volvulus: theatre. NEC: stop feeds, decompress, antibiotics.
HUS: no antibiotics for E. coli O157.

Def: Haematemesis: confirm the blood is the child's own and GI.
Cause: Non-variceal: oesophagitis, gastritis, peptic ulcer (H. pylori, NSAIDs), Mallory-Weiss, button battery.
Variceal: portal hypertension after umbilical venous catheterisation (portal vein thrombosis), biliary atresia.
Neonate: swallowed maternal blood, vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
Patho: Portal vein thrombosis → pre-hepatic portal hypertension → varices.
Button battery → necrosis within hours → can erode into the aorta.
Signs: Splenomegaly, ascites, caput medusae, thrombocytopenia → variceal.
Neonate bleeding from several sites → vitamin K deficiency.
Dx: Exclude impostors: epistaxis, cracked nipple (Apt test), red foods.
Split variceal vs non-variceal - decides treatment.
Rx: Two large cannulas, cross-match, blood; vitamin K + FFP for coagulopathy.
Variceal: terlipressin or octreotide + prophylactic antibiotics + band ligation.
Non-variceal: high-dose proton pump inhibitor + endoscopy; button battery → emergency removal.

Def: Proteinuria: is it real, is it big? Leukocyturia = UTI until culture negative.
Cause: Commonest: transient proteinuria; orthostatic (upright only, overweight adolescents).
Nephrotic age 1-10 → minimal change disease (~90%).
Sterile pyuria: partially treated UTI, renal tuberculosis, Kawasaki disease, appendicitis.
Patho: Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria, oedema, albumin below 30 g/L, hyperlipidaemia.
PSGN: low C3, normal C4, normal by 8 weeks; follows pharyngitis by 1-2 weeks, skin by 3-6 weeks.
Signs: Nephrotic complications: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, renal vein thrombosis, PE.
Nephritic: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, milder proteinuria.
Dx: Start with urinalysis; confirm on first-morning urine; quantify with protein:creatinine ratio.
UTI: nitrites specific, leucocyte esterase sensitive; nephritic → complement, ASOT.
After UTI: ultrasound → MCUG (VCUG), DMSA.
Rx: Typical nephrotic 1-10 y → steroids without biopsy.
Nephritic → urgent nephrology.

Def: Haematuria: confirm red cells on microscopy via urinalysis, then glomerular vs non-glomerular.
Cause: Glomerular: IgA, post-streptococcal GN, HSP, Alport, thin BM, MPGN/lupus, HUS.
Non-glomerular: UTI (commonest overall), stones, trauma, Wilms, coagulopathy, sickle cell.
Patho: Red cell casts prove haematuria is glomerular in origin.
IgA 1-2 days after URTI, normal complement; post-strep 1-3 weeks, low C3.
Signs: Glomerular: brown or cola-coloured, without clots, proteinuria, hypertension.
Initial haematuria = urethral; terminal = bladder or prostate.
Alport: sensorineural deafness and family history of renal failure.
Dx: Dipstick positive with no red cells → myoglobinuria or haemoglobinuria; exclude beetroot, rifampicin.
Glomerular: check complement levels; BP, protein dipstick, renal function, ultrasound.
Rx: Red cell casts → glomerular work-up; stop looking at the bladder.
Non-glomerular → target cause: UTI, stones, trauma, tumour (Wilms spreads to lungs).

Def: Involuntary voiding at age ≥ 5: at least 2 times/week for ≥ 3 months; primary vs secondary.
Cause: Greatest risk factor: family history; both parents → ~70%.
Secondary: UTI, diabetes mellitus, DI, CKD, constipation, stress/abuse, neuro, structural.
Patho: Failure to wake, nocturnal polyuria (low ADH), small bladder capacity.
Constipation compresses the bladder, causing detrusor overactivity.
Signs: Continuous dampness in a toilet-trained girl → ectopic ureter.
Sacral dimple/hairy patch → spinal dysraphism; polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss → DM.
Dx: First rule out organic causes: dipstick everyone for infection, glucose, specific gravity.
Examine lumbosacral spine, gait, lower-limb reflexes.
Rx: First-line: lifestyle modification and behavioral training (night fluid restriction, timed voiding).
Next: enuresis alarm ± oral desmopressin; imipramine rarely used.
Desmopressin → restrict evening fluids (hyponatraemia); the alarm is the best long-term cure.

Def: True polyuria: >2 l/m²/day, with polydipsia.
Cause: Three causes: osmotic diuresis (diabetes mellitus), diabetes insipidus, primary polydipsia.
Central DI: craniopharyngioma, germinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, trauma.
Nephrogenic: AVPR2, low K, high Ca, lithium.
Patho: Central = no ADH; nephrogenic = kidney ignores ADH.
Primary polydipsia → low-normal serum osmolality.
Signs: Glycosuria, weight loss despite appetite, ketones → DM.
DI: high serum osmolality with dilute urine.
Dx: First bedside test: urine dipstick for glucose; then paired serum + urine osmolality.
Water deprivation test: stop at 3-5% body-weight loss.
Concentrates after desmopressin → central DI → MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
Rx: Central DI: desmopressin + assess other pituitary hormones (cortisol).
Nephrogenic: free water, low-solute diet, thiazides, sometimes indometacin (indomethacin).

topics.title: Differential diagnosis and treatment of hypertension. Pheochromocytoma.

Def: BP ≥ 95th centile for age, sex, height, confirmed on 3 occasions.
Pheochromocytoma: tumor of chromaffin cells; rule of 10s.
Cause: Before adolescence most often kidney disease (~70-80%), then renovascular, coarctation, endocrine, drugs.
ARPKD (infants, PKHD1); ADPKD (young adults, renin).
Pheochromocytoma: MEN 2A/2B, VHL, NF1, SDH; familial more often bilateral.
Patho: Catecholamine-secreting tumour → episodic surges.
Beta-blocker first → unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis.
Neuroblastoma (adrenal medulla): N-myc, Homer-Wright rosettes.
Signs: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; fasting hyperglycemia.
Weak femorals → coarctation; hypertension + bradycardia = Cushing triad.
MEN 2B: tall, kyphoscoliosis, lip neuromas.
Dx: Cuff bladder covers 80% of arm; too small raises reading; BP in all four limbs.
Pheo: metanephrines → adrenal CT/MRI → I-123 MIBG scan.
Ultrasound for PKD; string of beads = fibromuscular dysplasia.
Rx: Pheo: alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine), then beta-blockade, then surgical excision.
Hyperkinetic hypertension: beta-blocker; Cushing triad: do not lower BP.

topics.title: Differential diagnosis and treatment of cough in children

Def: Acute cough under 3 weeks; chronic cough lasts more than 4 weeks.
Cause: Acute: viral infection of the respiratory tract commonest; bronchiolitis (RSV), croup, foreign body.
Chronic: pertussis, asthma, GERD, cystic fibrosis, protracted bacterial bronchitis, primary ciliary dyskinesia.
Patho: Bronchiolitis: small airway inflammation, usually RSV.
Pertussis: catarrhal 1-2 weeks → paroxysmal → convalescent; coughing risks pneumothorax.
Chronic wet cough + clubbing → suppurative lung disease, never asthma.
Signs: Bronchiolitis: wheezing/crackles, not stridor. Pertussis: whoop, post-tussive vomiting; infants apnoea and cyanosis.
Barking → croup; nocturnal dry + wheeze → asthma; meconium ileus → CF.
Sudden cough in a well toddler → foreign body.
Dx: Plot growth, check clubbing, immunisations, choking history, TB contacts.
Suspected foreign body → rigid bronchoscopy; normal CXR doesn't exclude.
Rx: Viral: reassure + safety-net; no over-the-counter cough medicines.
Bronchiolitis: supportive; RSV prevention nirsevimab or palivizumab.
Pertussis: macrolide, also prophylaxis for contacts.

topics.title: Sore throat (viral versus bacterial pharyngitis) and upper respiratory tract infection

Def: About 70-80% of sore throats in children are viral; the task is finding group A strep.
Cause: Viruses; EBV in teenagers; strep in age 3-14.
Emergencies: epiglottitis, quinsy, retropharyngeal abscess, diphtheria, Lemierre syndrome.
Patho: Untreated strep → acute rheumatic fever; antibiotics do not prevent PSGN.
Cough, coryza or hoarseness = viral.
Signs: Strep: abrupt fever, exudate, tender nodes, no cough; EBV: posterior nodes, splenomegaly.
Quinsy: trismus, uvula deviated away; epiglottitis: drooling, muffled voice, tripod, no cough.
Dx: Rapid strep has low sensitivity: negative → throat culture.
EBV: atypical lymphocytes, raised LFTs; diphtheria: gray-white pseudomembrane.
Rx: Strep: penicillin V for 10 days, to prevent rheumatic fever.
EBV given amoxicillin → non-allergic maculopapular rash; no contact sport 4-6 weeks (splenic rupture).

Def: Inspiratory stridor localises narrowing above the cords (extrathoracic); acute cause is usually croup.
Cause: Croup: parainfluenza virus, age 6 months to 6 years.
Mimics: epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis (Staph aureus), foreign body, laryngomalacia, vascular ring.
Patho: The subglottis swells inward because it is ringed by the cricoid, the only complete cartilage ring.
Signs: Croup: barking cough, stridor, not toxic; laryngomalacia: improves prone.
Epiglottitis: drooling, toxic, no cough; tracheitis: toxic, no response to adrenaline.
Dx: Severity = stridor at rest, recession, conscious level, not oxygen saturation.
Epiglottitis: do not examine the throat.
Rx: Every child with croup gets oral dexamethasone; severe: nebulised adrenaline, wears off in about 2 hours.
Epiglottitis: secure the airway first; foreign body: rigid bronchoscopy.

Def: Haemolysis is proven by anaemia with high reticulocytes, high unconjugated bilirubin, high LDH, low haptoglobin.
Cause: Positive direct Coombs = immune: warm AIHA IgG, cold AIHA IgM.
Coombs negative: hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD, sickle cell, thalassaemia, HUS/TTP/DIC.
Patho: Hereditary spherocytosis: membrane tethering defect, autosomal dominant.
G6PD: triggered by infection, fava beans, drugs → bite cells, Heinz bodies.
Signs: Jaundice, splenomegaly, dark urine; sickle cell: dactylitis, acute chest syndrome.
Low reticulocytes in chronic haemolysis = parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.
Dx: Spherocytes, Coombs negative, positive EMA binding, raised MCHC = hereditary spherocytosis.
Schistocytes = microangiopathic haemolysis; Hb electrophoresis for sickle and thalassaemia.
Rx: Warm AIHA: stop offending drug, steroids; splenectomy last resort.
Sickle: daily penicillin to 5 years; fever → ceftriaxone; stroke or priapism → exchange transfusion.

Def: The first branch point in any anaemia is the MCV; the commonest in childhood is iron deficiency.
Cause: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, lead poisoning.
Macrocytic: B12/folate deficiency, Diamond-Blackfan; pancytopenia: Fanconi, aplastic anaemia.
Patho: Excess cow's milk: iron-poor, inhibits iron absorption, occult GI blood loss.
B12/folate are needed for DNA synthesis, so cells grow large.
Signs: Lead: bluish gum-tooth line, LEAD mnemonic; B12: paresthesias, megaloblasts.
Fanconi: short stature, café-au-lait spots, malformed thumbs.
Dx: RDW high in iron deficiency, normal in thalassaemia trait; red cell count normal or high.
Ferritin is an acute phase protein, so inflammation can mask deficiency.
Rx: Iron deficiency: oral elemental iron, continued 3 months after Hb normalises.
Lead 45-69: DMSA (succimer); ≥ 70 mcg/dL: IM dimercaprol + EDTA.

Def: Failure to thrive classically means crossing two or more weight centile lines downward.
Cause: Commonest cause: inadequate intake (non-organic); child neglect is the commonest maltreatment.
Organic: cystic fibrosis, galactosaemia, congenital heart disease, enteropeptidase deficiency.
Patho: Order of loss: weight → height → head circumference.
Congenital heart disease: increased energy expenditure plus reduced intake.
Signs: Short and plump with delayed bone age suggests an endocrine cause.
Small head from early on: intrauterine, genetic or congenital infection.
Kwashiorkor: oedema, swollen abdomen; marasmus: wasting.
Dx: Highest-yield 'investigation': observe a feed.
Meconium ileus → cystic fibrosis; neonatal jaundice and E. coli sepsis → galactosaemia.
Rx: Treat the cause; feeding advice for intake problems.
Suspected abuse: first contact child protective services (CPS).

Def: Enlarged liver, spleen or both; a palpable liver edge is normal in infants, so measure the liver span.
Cause: EBV/infectious mononucleosis, CMV, hepatitis A, malaria, visceral leishmaniasis.
Hereditary spherocytosis, systemic JIA, glycogen storage disease type I.
Patho: A spleen must enlarge to about 2-3 times normal size before it is palpable.
Hypersplenism: enlarged spleen sequesters blood cells and lowers the platelet count.
Signs: Infant hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycaemia suggests von Gierke.
CMV newborn: blueberry muffin rash, jaundice; systemic JIA: spiking fevers, salmon-pink rash.
Dx: First test: full blood count and film.
Synthetic function: prothrombin time (INR), not the ALT.
Rx: Treat the cause.
EBV splenomegaly: avoid contact sports for 4-6 weeks.

Def: In acute diarrhoea the priority is assessing hydration, not the stool.
Cause: Acute: mostly rotavirus and norovirus; bacterial if bloody.
Chronic: pivotal question is whether the child is growing; toddler's diarrhoea is the thriving form.
Patho: ORS works because the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) stays intact.
Antibiotics in E. coli O157 raise the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Osmotic diarrhoea stops with fasting; secretory continues.
Signs: Loose stools with recognisable food in a thriving 2-year-old = toddler's diarrhoea.
Blood, high fever, severe pain suggest bacterial cause.
Dx: Grade dehydration clinically.
Faltering growth: coeliac screen with tTG and total IgA, sweat test, calprotectin.
Rx: ORS and continue feeding; IV only if ORS fails.
Loperamide is not used; no routine antibiotics.

Def: Green (bilious) vomit means obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater.
Cause: Neonate: malrotation with volvulus, atresias, Hirschsprung, salt-wasting CAH.
Infant: pyloric stenosis, intussusception; older: gastroenteritis, appendicitis, DKA, raised ICP.
Patho: Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Urine is acidic despite alkalosis: paradoxical aciduria.
Signs: Pyloric stenosis: 2-8 weeks, firstborn boy, projectile vomiting, hungry afterwards.
Neonate with shock, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia = salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Dx: Bilious vomiting: urgent exclusion of malrotation with volvulus.
Pyloric stenosis imaging of choice: ultrasonography.
Rx: Correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery; alkalosis risks post-operative apnoea.
Operation: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy; volvulus → emergency surgery.

Def: The commonest cause of an acute abdomen in children is appendicitis.
Cause: Sort by age: neonate NEC and volvulus; toddler intussusception; school age appendicitis.
Adolescent: testicular or ovarian torsion, gynaecological causes; trauma: splenic rupture.
Patho: Pain starts periumbilically: appendix is a midgut organ, afferents enter the cord at T10.
Two-stage splenic rupture: subcapsular haematoma, shock hours to days later.
Signs: Neonate with bilious vomiting = malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise.
Appendicitis: central pain moving to RLQ, anorexia, low fever.
Dx: Four free checks: chest, urine dipstick, glucose, scrotum in boys.
Polytraumatised child: acute (whole-body) CT.
Rx: Peritonism → surgical referral; resuscitate if unstable.
Salvage of a torted testis falls sharply after about 6 hours.

topics.title: Differential diagnosis of palpable abdominal mass in childhood

Def: Exclude benign causes, then separate Wilms tumour from neuroblastoma.
Cause: Neonate: most masses are renal (hydronephrosis, multicystic dysplastic kidney).
Wilms: WAGR (aniridia), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hemihypertrophy; neuroblastoma: neural crest, N-myc.
Patho: Wilms arises from metanephric mesenchyme (blastema); it spreads mostly to the lungs.
Do not palpate repeatedly: risk of rupture.
Signs: Wilms: peaks 3-4 years, well child, smooth mass, does not cross the midline, haematuria.
Neuroblastoma: under 2 years, unwell, crosses midline, raccoon eyes, opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.
Dx: Abdominal ultrasound first.
Neuroblastoma: raised urinary VMA and HVA; small blue round cells, Homer-Wright rosettes.
Rx: A suspected Wilms tumour must not be repeatedly palpated.
Europe (SIOP): chemotherapy before surgery; US (COG): usually operate first.

Def: Most chronic abdominal pain in children is functional and should be diagnosed positively.
Cause: Functional: irritable bowel syndrome, functional abdominal pain.
Organic: constipation is the commonest treatable cause; also coeliac, IBD, H. pylori, choledochal cyst, abuse.
Patho: The further the pain from the umbilicus, the more likely an organic cause.
IBS is not related to structural abnormalities.
Signs: Functional abdominal pain never wakes the child at night.
Key question in infancy: how the infant is growing/developing.
Dx: Best non-invasive test to separate IBD from functional pain: faecal calprotectin.
H. pylori is urease-positive: urea breath test.
Rx: IBS first line: lifestyle modification, low FODMAP diet, fiber.
Best evidence: cognitive behavioural therapy; treat constipation.

Def: Four Starling mechanisms: raised hydrostatic pressure, low oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction.
Cause: Commonest cause of generalised oedema in a young child: nephrotic syndrome.
Also kwashiorkor, protein-losing enteropathy, liver disease, hereditary angio-oedema.
Patho: Kwashiorkor: oedema from decreased plasma oncotic pressure.
Membranous nephropathy: GBM thickening, granular immune-complex deposits; amyloid deposits in the mesangium.
Signs: Oedema first appears periorbitally, in the morning.
Recurrent non-pitting, non-itchy swelling without urticaria suggests hereditary angio-oedema.
Dx: Nephrotic: UPCR >200 mg/mmol, low albumin.
Low albumin with a negative urine dipstick points to the gut (protein-losing enteropathy) or liver.
Rx: Treat the mechanism.
Nephrotic syndrome in children: mostly steroid-responsive; HAE is C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency.

topics.title: Differential diagnosis of dehydration in childhood

Def: Fluid deficit (ml) = % dehydration × weight (kg) × 10.
Cause: Commonest cause: acute gastroenteritis; rotavirus is the commonest cause of severe diarrhoea.
Cholera and Shigella (high fever, mucoid-bloody diarrhoea, seizures) also cause it.
Patho: Diarrhoea: ECF volume decreased, haematocrit and plasma protein increased.
Rotavirus causes villous destruction and atrophy.
Signs: Doughy skin in a dehydrated infant suggests hypernatraemic dehydration.
In children hypotension is a late, pre-terminal sign of shock.
Dx: Check serum sodium; correct slowly, no faster than 0.5 mEq/L/hr.
Hypernatraemia corrected rapidly causes cerebral oedema.
Rx: Without shock: ORS 50 ml/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance.
Shock bolus: 10 ml/kg 0.9% sodium chloride; rotavirus vaccine at 2, 4, 6 months.

topics.title: Principles of fluid therapy in childhood Maintenance fluid therapy plan for a 3kg neonate and for a 20kg child.

Def: Plan = resuscitation + deficit + maintenance + ongoing losses; standard maintenance is D5NS.
Cause: Holliday-Segar maintenance: 100 ml/kg first 10 kg, 50 ml/kg next 10 kg, 20 ml/kg above.
Patho: Hypotonic saline alone can cause RBC lysis; use isotonic fluid beyond the neonatal period.
Sodium is withheld from neonatal fluids until the postnatal diuresis begins.
Signs: Overload: oedema, hepatomegaly, crackles, weight gain.
High ADH (meningitis, pneumonia, post-op, head injury): restrict to 50-80%.
Dx: Maintenance for a 20 kg child: 1500 ml/day (≈60 ml/h); hourly 4/2/1 rule.
3 kg neonate day 1: about 180 ml/day (7.5 ml/h).
Rx: Term neonate day 1: 50-60 ml/kg/day of 10% glucose, rising to 120-150 ml/kg/day by day 5.
Older child: 0.9% NaCl with 5% glucose; shock bolus 10 ml/kg.

Def: Mismatch of chromosomal, gonadal or phenotypic sex; ambiguous genitalia is an emergency.
Cause: Commonest cause of ambiguous genitalia in a newborn: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CAH).
46,XY with female genitalia, testes and no uterus: complete androgen insensitivity.
Patho: SRY makes the gonad a testis; AMH from Sertoli cells regresses the Müllerian ducts.
Testosterone virilises; androgen insensitivity is an androgen receptor defect.
Signs: Salt-wasting CAH presents at 1-3 weeks with low sodium and high potassium.
Androgen insensitivity: pubic hair absent; Müllerian agenesis: present.
Dx: Do karyotype; screening test for CAH: raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
Non-palpable gonads in a 'male' infant = CAH until proven otherwise.
Rx: Involve the MDT before assigning sex.
Androgen insensitivity: bilateral gonadectomy after puberty; do not circumcise hypospadias.

Def: Premature puberty: signs before 8 years in girls, 9 in boys.
Delayed puberty: no breasts by 13, testes by 14.
Cause: Central precocious puberty: girls mostly idiopathic; boys often organic (CNS lesion).
Commonest delay: constitutional delay; Kallmann syndrome (anosmia); Turner and primary ovarian insufficiency.
Patho: Central: leuprolide stimulation increases LH; peripheral: LH/FSH suppressed.
Oestrogen closes the epiphyseal growth plate.
Signs: First sign: girls thelarche; boys testicular volume ≥4 ml.
Boy with small testes suggests CAH/adrenal cause.
Dx: Central precocious puberty needs MRI of the brain before treatment.
Primary amenorrhea: pelvic ultrasound; Müllerian agenesis has normal secondary sex characteristics.
Rx: Central precocious puberty: GnRH agonist depot (leuprolide).
Treat the cause; premature adrenarche and newborn breast enlargement need reassurance.

Def: Commonest symptomatic tachyarrhythmia in children: SVT; presents with abrupt onset tachycardia.
Cause: WPW: ventricular pre-excitation; long QT: Romano-Ward (AD), Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (AR, deafness).
Congenital complete heart block: maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies; Brugada: AD.
Patho: Long QT predisposes to torsades de pointes.
Adenosine inhibits the AV node, causing transient heart block.
Signs: Infants with SVT (rate >220) present with heart failure, not palpitations.
Sudden syncope without prodrome = arrhythmia.
Dx: WPW resting ECG: short PR, widened QRS, delta wave.
Brugada: pseudo-RBBB with ST elevation in V1-V3.
Rx: Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres first, then rapid IV adenosine; verapamil contraindicated in infants.
Unstable: synchronised cardioversion; long QT: beta-blockers; complete heart block: pacemaker.

Def: Excess weight judged by BMI centiles; mostly exogenous obesity.
Cause: Exogenous: child is tall with advanced bone age.
Endocrine: child is short with slowing height velocity; commonest monogenic cause MC4R; Prader-Willi.
Patho: Prader-Willi: gene deletion, raised ghrelin.
Insulin resistance underlies acanthosis nigricans, PCOS and fatty liver.
Signs: Velvety dark skin in neck folds = acanthosis nigricans.
Knee pain and limp in an obese teenager: SCFE; also obstructive sleep apnea.
Dx: Genetic red flags: onset before 5 years, severe hyperphagia, developmental delay or dysmorphism.
Metabolic syndrome: at least 3 of 5 criteria.
Rx: Family-based lifestyle change first.
GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide) licensed for obesity from age 12.

Def: Short stature = height below -2 SD.
Cause: Normal variants: familial, constitutional delay.
Most frequent endocrine cause: hypothyroidism; also growth hormone deficiency, Turner, Prader-Willi, Fanconi anaemia.
Patho: Growth hormone and thyroid hormone increase bone growth; GH raises IGF.
Pathological short stature = low height velocity, crossing centiles downward.
Signs: Familial: bone age equal to chronological age.
Constitutional delay: bone age delayed, final height normal.
Dx: Every unexplained short girl needs a karyotype to exclude Turner syndrome.
GH deficiency needs two GH stimulation tests.
Rx: Treat the cause: levothyroxine for hypothyroidism.
Growth hormone for deficiency, Turner and Prader-Willi; constitutional delay: reassurance.

topics.title: Muscle weakness, paralysis and other myopathies

Def: Localise the weakness: horn cell, nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle.
Cause: SMA: deletion of SMN1; Duchenne: X-linked absence of dystrophin.
Myasthenia: antibodies to postsynaptic ACh receptors; infant botulism: honey spores; GBS.
Patho: Myasthenia: weakness worsens with muscle use; Lambert-Eaton (presynaptic calcium channels) improves.
SMA severity depends on SMN2 copy number.
Signs: Tongue fasciculations and areflexia in a floppy infant: SMA; infant botulism begins with constipation.
Duchenne: Gowers sign; myasthenia: fatigable ptosis and diplopia.
Dx: GBS: CSF high protein with normal cell count; serial spirometry.
Duchenne: serum CK raised 10-100x; myotonic dystrophy: EMG then genetic testing.
Rx: GBS: IVIG or plasmapheresis; infant botulism: human-derived botulism immune globulin.
Duchenne: steroids; myasthenic crisis: intubation, then prednisone plus IVIG.

Def: Mucocutaneous bleeding suggests platelets/VWF; joint and muscle bleeds suggest clotting factors.
Cause: Haemophilia A = factor VIII; haemophilia B = factor IX.
Commonest inherited bleeding disorder: von Willebrand disease; ITP: IgG against GPIIb/IIIa.
Patho: Desmopressin increases release of vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies.
ITP antibodies are produced in the spleen and can cross the placenta.
Signs: ITP: scattered petechiae, isolated thrombocytopenia, increased bleeding time.
Severe haemophilia: spontaneous joint bleeds.
Dx: Haemophilia screen: APTT prolonged, PT normal.
Chronic ITP: low platelets for >1 year.
Rx: Haemophilia with head trauma, even without fainting: immediate factor concentrate and nearest haemophilia centre.
Inhibitors: bypassing agent; prophylaxis emicizumab; ITP with only petechiae: observation.

Def: ADHD: hyperactivity, impulsivity, and/or inattention in ≥ 2 settings.
Autism spectrum disorder: poor social interactions, repetitive / ritualized behaviors.
Cause: ADHD: ~70-80% heritable, prematurity, fetal alcohol/tobacco.
Autism: genetic; fragile X, Rett, fetal valproate; not MMR; more common in males.
Patho: ADHD: weak dopamine and noradrenaline signalling → impulsivity.
Autism: altered connectivity → social cues not rewarding → routines calm.
Signs: ADHD: onset before 12, in two or more settings, for at least 6 months.
Autism: early childhood onset; poor eye contact, insistence on sameness, stereotypies.
Dx: ADHD: clinical; exclude hearing, vision, absences, OSA.
Autism screening at 18 months and 2 years: M-CHAT-R/F (16-30 months).
Hearing test before diagnosing autism in non-verbal child; ADOS.
Rx: ADHD from age 5: stimulants ± CBT; methylphenidate first-line, then atomoxetine, guanfacine.
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, height and weight on stimulants.
Autism: early intensive developmental therapy; risperidone for severe irritability.

Def: Disturbed pH; follows the HCO3: pCO2 ratio.
SMORE: Same direction (pH and pCO2) → Metabolic; Opposite → RESpiratory.
Cause: High anion gap = acid added: DKA, lactate, renal failure, toxins.
Normal anion gap: diarrhoea, RTA (HARDASS); alkalosis: vomiting, diuretics.
Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Patho: Metabolic acidosis: decrease in HCO3 → hyperventilation → decreased pCO2.
Respiratory compensation is immediate; kidneys slow (3-5 days).
Pyloric stenosis: HCl loss + aldosterone → paradoxical aciduria.
Signs: Kussmaul breathing, vomiting, lethargy.
A normal or rising pCO2 in acute severe asthma signals exhaustion.
Dx: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3), normal about 8-12.
Winter's: expected pCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 (±2).
Metabolic alkalosis: next step check urine chloride.
Rx: Treat the cause: fluids, insulin for DKA, dialysis; bicarbonate not routine.
Pyloric: chloride + volume first.
Operate once Cl ⁻ and HCO3 normal.

Def: Abnormal plasma sodium → water shifts into (low) or out of (high) brain cells.
Cause: Low: SIADH + hypotonic fluids, diarrhoea and vomiting, salt-wasting CAH, nephrotic, heart failure.
High: gastroenteritis, poor breastfeeding in week 1, diabetes insipidus, bad formula.
Patho: In hyponatraemia water moves into brain cells, causing cerebral oedema.
High Na⁺ → brain shrinks → bridging veins tear → haemorrhage.
Signs: Low: headache, vomiting, seizures; neonate low Na⁺ + high K⁺ → CAH.
High: high-pitched cry, doughy skin, seizures; shock late.
Dx: Plasma and urine osmolality, urine Na, volume status.
SIADH: low plasma osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine, euvolaemia, urine Na >30.
Rx: Hyponatraemic seizures: bolus of 3% saline; SIADH → fluid restriction; isotonic maintenance fluids.
Too-rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination; raise ≤ 8-10 mmol/L/24 h.
Hypernatraemia: corrected over 48 hours, no more than 0.5 mmol/L per hour; 0.9% saline for shock.

Def: Abnormal K⁺; K⁺ sets the resting membrane potential.
Cause: High: AKI, CAH, DKA, tumour lysis, ACE inhibitors, heparin, trimethoprim.
Commonest cause of high K in a well infant: a haemolysed sample.
Low: diarrhoea and vomiting, pyloric stenosis, diuretics, insulin in DKA, refeeding.
Patho: High K⁺ → inactivates fast Na⁺ channels → slow conduction, fast repolarisation.
Salbutamol and insulin lower K by stimulating the Na/K-ATPase.
Low K may not correct until magnesium is replaced.
Signs: Earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia: peaked T waves → wide QRS → sine wave.
Low: weakness, ileus, flat T waves, U waves.
Dx: First exclude haemolysed heel-prick; repeat free-flowing venous sample.
Low K: urine K (>20 = renal loss), acid-base.
Rx: High with ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate 10% first (protect).
Shift: salbutamol, insulin-glucose, sodium bicarbonate; then resin, loop diuretic, dialysis.
Low: oral KCl; IV in fluids, never bolus; replace Mg.

Def: Abnormal amniotic fluid: poly AFI >24-25 cm; oligo AFI under 5 cm.
Cause: Poly: oesophageal and duodenal atresia, maternal diabetes (fetal osmotic diuresis), TTTS recipient.
Oligo: no urine (renal agenesis, ARPKD), blocked (PUV), leak (PPROM, commonest), FGR.
ACE inhibitors / ARBs in utero may cause oligohydramnios.
Patho: After 20 weeks fluid comes mainly from fetal urine, removed by fetal swallowing.
Early oligohydramnios → no lung distension → lethal pulmonary hypoplasia.
Signs: Poly: preterm labour, cord prolapse, placental abruption after rapid decompression.
Oligo: Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, twisted facies, extremity deformities, renal agenesis).
Also growth restriction, cord compression.
Dx: Ultrasound AFI; double bubble (duodenal atresia), keyhole bladder (PUV).
Oligo before ~24 weeks → most severe lung hypoplasia.
Rx: Polyhydramnios newborn: NG tube before first feed to exclude oesophageal atresia.
Severe polyhydramnios: amnioreduction or indomethacin; term, mild, asymptomatic: expectant.
Oligohydramnios: treat cause; pulmonary hypoplasia is the killer.

Def: Newborn arrest is respiratory - aerate the lungs.
Best indicator of success: the heart rate.
Cause: Hypoxia → primary apnoea → gasping → terminal apnoea.
Meconium aspiration: term and post-term infants.
Patho: First breaths clear lung fluid, create FRC → pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
Meconium inactivates surfactant; bradycardia = hypoxia until proven otherwise.
Signs: Assess tone, breathing, heart rate; HR under 100 or not breathing → act.
Apgar at 1 and 5 minutes: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration.
Dx: Stethoscope, then ECG/pre-ductal SpO₂.
Targets: 70-75% at 3 min, 80-85% at 5 min, 85-95% at 10 min.
PPV with brighter left chest transillumination → left pneumothorax.
Rx: Dry, warm; 5 inflation breaths, each 2-3 seconds; term babies start in air (21%).
Compressions 3:1 if HR under 60/min after 30 s effective ventilation.
Adrenaline 20 µg/kg via UVC; HIE: 33-34 °C for 72 h, within 6 h.

Def: Paediatric arrest = end of progressive hypoxia or shock.
Key to survival: elapsed time to effective resuscitation.
Cause: Respiratory failure or shock → tiring → hypoxia → bradycardia → asystole.
Non-shockable rhythms (asystole, PEA) are commonest.
Patho: Paradoxical breathing: chest moves inward, abdomen outward during inhalation.
PEA: organized rhythm without a palpable pulse.
Signs: ABCDE: stridor, recession, grunting, head bobbing, CRT, AVPU, glucose.
Dx: Pulse oximetry not informative in carbon monoxide intoxication, methaemoglobinaemia, severe anaemia, cardiac failure, cold extremities.
SpO₂ ignores ventilation → capnography or blood gas.
Rx: Conscious, breathing: face mask with reservoir, high flow 10-15 l/min.
BLS: 5 rescue breaths, then 15:2; asystole/PEA: CPR + adrenaline 10 µg/kg IV/IO every 3-5 min.
VF / pulseless VT: unsynchronized shock 4 J/kg; amiodarone after 3rd and 5th shock.

topics.title: Fever, management of fever, antipyretics, pain relief

Def: Fever: cytokine-driven rise in hypothalamic set point.
Cause: Microbial products → IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α release.
Early-onset neonatal sepsis occurs within 72 hours of birth.
Patho: Cytokines induce PGE₂ in the hypothalamus, raising the set point → shivering, vasoconstriction.
Antipyretics block COX; fever itself not harmful.
Signs: NICE red: child under 3 months with temperature ≥ 38 °C, mottled, grunting, neck stiffness.
Amber: 3-6 months with ≥ 39 °C, fever ≥ 5 days, CRT ≥ 3 s.
Dx: NICE traffic light for under-5s; red → septic work-up.
Neonatal sepsis: blood culture, serial CRP, lumbar puncture; antibiotics within 1 hour.
Pain scales: FLACC (preverbal), Wong-Baker (4+), numeric (8+).
Rx: Only if distressed: paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4-6 h, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg three times daily.
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures; aspirin avoided under 16 (Reye syndrome).
Neonatal sepsis: ampicillin + gentamicin; codeine contraindicated under 12 (CYP2D6).

Def: Inadequate oxygen delivery; types hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive, dissociative.
Cause: Gastroenteritis, haemorrhage, sepsis, anaphylaxis, myocarditis, SVT, tamponade.
Neonate 1-2 weeks with weak femoral pulses: duct-dependent lesion.
Patho: Children compensate with tachycardia + vasoconstriction until 30-40% volume lost.
Hypotension is a late sign of shock; tachycardia is early.
Signs: Tachycardia (earliest), CRT >2 s, cool mottled peripheries, oliguria, lactic acidosis.
Bradycardia + hypotension = decompensation / pre-arrest.
Dx: Cultures, gas, lactate, glucose.
Hypotension in children 1-10 y: systolic below 70 + 2 × age mmHg.
Reassess HR, CRT, BP, liver edge, crackles after each bolus.
Rx: Septic shock: O2, IV/IO, fluid bolus 20 ml/kg body weight; antibiotics within 1 hour.
Fluid-refractory: start adrenaline or noradrenaline; TSS: clindamycin suppresses toxin synthesis.
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first (150 µg under 6); duct-dependent: prostaglandin E.

Def: Injuries from delivery, determined by anatomical layer and nerve root.
Cause: Risk factors: difficult deliveries, shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, vacuum, forceps.
Maternal hyperglycemia → macrosomia.
Patho: Caput succedaneum crosses suture lines; cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal and does not.
Subgaleal haemorrhage: injury to emissary veins, between aponeurosis and periosteum.
Erb: lateral traction on neck during delivery.
Signs: Cephalhaematoma: swelling limited to one cranial bone; resorption can cause jaundice.
Subgaleal haemorrhage: hypovolaemic shock, typically after vacuum delivery.
Erb C5-C6 waiter's tip; Klumpke C8-T1 claw hand ± Horner; clavicle: crepitus, asymmetric Moro.
Dx: Subgaleal: monitor head circumference, haemoglobin.
Erb palsy with tachypnoea suggests phrenic nerve palsy (C3-C5).
Clavicle fracture: check subclavian artery, brachial plexus.
Rx: Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts (flex hips) + suprapubic pressure.
Commonest fracture: clavicle, heals rapidly; plexus palsy resolves within 3 months (80%).
No biceps recovery by 3-6 months → surgery; subgaleal: volume and blood replacement.

Def: Ingestion: accidental in toddlers (1-4 y), deliberate in adolescents.
Cause: Medicines, cleaners, button batteries, paracetamol, iron, TCAs, opioids, caustics.
Lead poisoning: homes built before 1978.
Patho: Paracetamol: toxic metabolite NAPQI, detoxified by glutathione until exhausted.
Iron: corrosive, then mitochondrial poison; TCA: Na⁺ channel block → wide QRS.
Signs: Toxidromes: anticholinergic, cholinergic, opioid (pinpoint pupils), sympathomimetic.
Paracetamol day 1 near asymptomatic; lead: bluish gum-tooth line.
Aspirin: early pure respiratory alkalosis; late mixed with metabolic acidosis.
Dx: ABCDE + glucose; dose in mg/kg, assume worst case.
Paracetamol level on nomogram from 4 hours; iron X-ray + serum iron; battery CXR halo.
Lead: capillary level raised → measure venous lead level.
Rx: Never induce vomiting; charcoal only within 1 hour, does not bind iron, lithium, alcohols.
Antidotes: N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol); desferrioxamine (iron); bicarbonate (TCA); naloxone (opioid).
Oesophageal battery or coin: urgent endoscopy; lead moderate DMSA, severe dimercaprol + EDTA.

topics.title: Child abuse and shaken baby syndrome

Def: Physical, sexual, emotional abuse or neglect; neglect is the commonest form of maltreatment.
Cause: Most significant parental risk factor: being abused themselves; abuser usually primary caregiver.
Shaken baby: infants under 1 y, peak 2-4 months; sexual abuse peak 9-12 years.
Patho: Shaking tears the bridging veins, causing subdural haemorrhage.
Vitreous pulls retina → retinal haemorrhages; grip → posterior rib fractures.
Signs: History: delay, changing story, injury not fitting development.
Any bruise in a non-mobile infant; scalds with sharp lines of demarcation.
Abusive head trauma: subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy.
Dx: CT then MRI, skeletal survey repeated at 11-14 days, ophthalmology, coagulation.
Most specific: posterior rib and classic metaphyseal (corner) fractures.
Rx: Suspected abuse: contact child protective services first; abuse and neglect both reported.
Document exactly, keep child safe - admit if needed; welfare overrides confidentiality.

topics.title: Airway foreign bodies in children, aspiration

Def: Inhaled object in larynx, trachea or bronchus.
Cause: Toddlers 1-3 y: no molars, eat while running; nuts classic.
Right lung commonest: its bronchus is wider and more vertical.
Patho: Partial block = check valve → air trapped on expiration.
Complete block → atelectasis; nuts radiolucent.
Signs: Choking → symptom-free interval → cough, unilateral wheeze, recurrent pneumonia.
Laryngotracheal: stridor, cyanosis.
Dx: Holzknecht sign = pendulum movement of the mediastinum = airway foreign body.
Expiratory and inspiratory chest radiograph or fluoroscopy; normal X-ray never excludes.
Rx: Choking infant under 1 year: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts (not abdominal).
Over 1 y: abdominal thrusts.
Definitive: rigid bronchoscopy; symptomatic swallowed coin: emergency endoscopy.

Def: Imaging chosen by ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable): justification, optimisation, non-ionising first.
Cause: Children radiosensitive: dividing cells, longer remaining life, organs close to beam.
Patho: Blood echogenic, CSF anechoic → cranial US via anterior fontanelle.
Preterm IVH arises in the germinal matrix.
Signs: Thymus shadow visible till 3 years of age; absent → DiGeorge or SCID.
Mediastinal shadow narrowing trachea → mass, not thymus.
Dx: Ultrasound first, MRI next; cranial US: brain haemorrhage and hydrocephalus.
Urinary: US, MCUG, DMSA 4-6 months after infection shows scars, MAG3.
Rx: Polytrauma → acute CT; head trauma: non-contrast CT if GCS ≤ 14 or skull fracture.
Suspected stroke with normal CT → MRI / MR angiography.
US for pyloric stenosis, intussusception; upper GI contrast for bilious vomiting.
· Thesis line

topics.title: Standard and recommended immunizations for children and adolescents

Def: Vaccines prime memory B and T cells → fast high-affinity IgG on real infection.
Cause: Live: MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG; avoid in SCID, pregnancy.
Hungary: BCG to all newborns; varicella mandatory since 2019.
Patho: Maternal antibodies neutralise MMR earlier → given after 12 months.
Conjugate vaccines work in infants because the protein carrier recruits T-helper cells.
Signs: MMR fever and rash appear 7-12 days after vaccination.
Varicella vaccine rash with few lesions = vaccine-strain replication.
Dx: Only universal contraindication: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component.
DTaP: anaphylaxis → no future doses; encephalopathy → hold pertussis.
Not contraindications: mild illness; preterms use chronological age.
Rx: At 2, 4, 6 months: DTaP, IPV, PCV15, rotavirus; hepatitis B at birth, 2, 6 months.
MMR and varicella at 1 year and 4 years; annual influenza from 6 months.
Age 11: Tdap, meningococcal, HPV through 26.

topics.title: Normal psychomotor development in childhood (different age groups). Child growth percentiles. Anthropometry.

Def: Development in 4 domains: gross motor, fine motor/vision, speech/hearing, social.
Cause: Any loss of skills is an urgent red flag.
Hand preference before 12 months is a red flag.
Patho: Myelination → cephalocaudal and proximal→distal progression.
Primitive reflexes normal till 6-12 months; persistence suggests upper motor neuron lesion (e.g. CP).
Signs: Social smile 6 weeks; lifts head 2 months; rolls over 6 months.
Sits alone, stranger anxiety 9 months; pulls to stand 9-12 months.
Walks 12-18 months (limit 18 months); kicks ball 2 years.
Dx: Weight, length, head circumference on centile charts; judge trajectory.
Growth failure: weight below 5th percentile or crossing two major lines.
Failure to thrive: weight → height → head circumference.
Rx: Birth weight regained by 2 weeks, doubles by 4-5 months, triples by 12 months.
Length rises 50% by 1 year; growth velocity is the most sensitive marker.

topics.title: Anthropometry of a newborn. Intrauterin growth restriction (IUGR). Characteristics of a premature baby.

Def: Term birth weight 2500-4000 g, head circumference ~35 cm; preterm under 37 weeks.
SGA = birth weight below the 10th centile for gestation.
Cause: Leading cause of low birth weight in developed countries: smoking.
Asymmetric FGR usually placental insufficiency; fetal: trisomies, TORCH.
Patho: Asymmetric (late, placental): head spared; symmetric (1st trimester infection): global growth lag.
Chronic hypoxia → EPO → polycythaemia (haematocrit over 65%) → hyperviscosity, jaundice.
Signs: IUGR: hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, polycythaemia.
Preterm: thin red skin, lanugo, soft ears, hypotonia.
RDS (surfactant deficiency), IVH, PDA, NEC, ROP.
Dx: Low birth weight under 2500 g; VLBW under 1500; ELBW under 1000 g.
Gestation by dating ultrasound, New Ballard score.
FGR: Doppler of umbilical artery; absent/reversed end-diastolic flow → urgent delivery.
Rx: Before birth: maternal glucocorticoids (24-34 wk) + MgSO4; after birth: artificial surfactant.
NEC: NPO, NG tube, IV fluids, antibiotics; surgery for perforation.
ROP: laser photocoagulation.

topics.title: Nutrition of the healthy infant: breastfeeding and weaning. Breastmilk composition. Energy requirements.

Def: Breastfeed on demand, exclusively for 6 months, continue to 2 years.
Cause: Contraindications: infant galactosaemia; maternal HIV, untreated tuberculosis, varicella.
Hepatitis B and mastitis are not.
Patho: Suckling → prolactin (synthesis) + oxytocin (let-down); supply follows demand.
Breast milk protein is one third of cow's; colostrum contains IgA.
Signs: Adequacy: ≥ 5 wet diapers per day at 5 days; loses up to 10% of birth weight.
Birth weight regained by 2 weeks.
Breast milk jaundice: β-glucuronidase.
Dx: Cow's milk first given after 12 months → else iron deficiency, renal solute load.
Energy ~100-110 kcal/kg/day early; fluid ~150 ml/kg/day.
Kwashiorkor: oedema, swollen abdomen; marasmus: wasting.
Rx: Solids not before 17 weeks, ~6 months; no honey under 12 months (infant botulism).
Breastfeeding jaundice: feed more often (q2h); milk jaundice: continue.
All: vitamin D 400 IU daily + vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth.

topics.title: Psychosomatic diseases. Anorexia nervosa Bulimia nervosa.

Def: Psychosomatic = real symptoms driven by stress; commonest: functional abdominal pain.
Anorexia: restriction, low weight; bulimia: binge + compensation weekly for 3 months.
Cause: Stress: school, bullying, family conflict, abuse; separation anxiety → school avoidance.
Anorexia peaks in adolescent girls.
Patho: Stress → HPA + brain-gut axis → visceral hypersensitivity.
Anorexia: loss of pulsatile GnRH → low LH/FSH/estrogen → amenorrhea.
Vomiting → HCl loss + aldosterone.
Signs: AN: bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo, amenorrhea, mitral valve prolapse.
BN: parotid hypertrophy, enamel erosion, Russell sign (knuckle calluses).
Conversion: la belle indifférence.
Dx: Exclude red flags; avoid endless tests.
BN: hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.
Admit AN: HR under 40, SBP under 80, temp under 35.5 °C, %mBMI under 70%, syncope.
Rx: Family-based therapy first-line for adolescent AN; bulimia: psychotherapy ± SSRIs (fluoxetine).
Refeeding: key electrolyte disturbance hypophosphataemia.
Somatic symptoms: monthly visits with a single physician; screen self-harm.

Def: Screening for diseases silent at birth, harmful, treatable (Wilson-Jungner).
Cause: Hungary screens 26 congenital metabolic diseases: PKU, hypothyroidism, galactosaemia, biotinidase + tandem-MS.
Aminoacidopathies, fatty-acid oxidation defects (MCAD), organic acidurias.
Patho: Placenta clears toxic metabolites in utero → feeding unmasks the defect.
PKU: deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase.
Galactosaemia: jaundice, cataract, E. coli sepsis after milk feeds.
Signs: MCAD: fasting → hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, sudden death.
PKU: fair skin, musty odour.
Dx: Heel prick at 48-72 hours → tandem mass spectrometry on dried blood spot, TSH, enzyme assays.
Positive screen ≠ diagnosis → urgent recall + confirmation.
Also hearing, pulse oximetry, hips, red reflex; vision every well-child visit (amblyopia).
Rx: PKU low-phe diet; galactosaemia stop lactose; MCAD avoid fasting.
All newborns receive vitamin K to prevent haemorrhagic disease; vitamin D 400 IU.
Hepatitis B mother: immune globulin + vaccine within 12 hours.

topics.title: Sudden infant death syndrome. Infantile and paediatric mortality data.

Def: SIDS is sudden death under 1 year, a diagnosis of exclusion after autopsy, scene investigation, history.
Cause: Smoking, bed-sharing (sofa, alcohol), prone/side sleep, soft bedding, overheating, prematurity.
Low birth weight: less than 2500 grams (5.5 pounds).
Patho: Triple-risk model: vulnerable infant + critical developmental period + external stressor.
Prone → rebreathes CO2 → hypoxia → vulnerable infant fails to arouse.
Signs: SIDS peaks at 2-4 months of age, during sleep.
More often boys, winter, preterm, low birth weight.
Dx: Unexpected death → full autopsy + skeletal survey, metabolic screen; exclude infection, MCAD, abuse.
Infant deaths: perinatal conditions (prematurity) and congenital malformations; over 1 year, accidents 36-40%.
Rx: “Back to sleep” (supine), avoid bed sharing, smoking cessation, pacifier during sleep.
Room-share in own cot, firm mattress; breastfeed, immunise; bereavement support.
Accident prevention: car seats, pool fencing, locked medicines.

topics.title: Clinical symptoms of infections, laboratory diagnostics, normal parameters.

Def: Infection signs are mostly the host response: fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, poor perfusion.
Cause: Any infant under 3 months with temperature ≥38 °C is high risk (NICE red); mottled skin, non-blanching rash.
Patho: IL-1, IL-6, TNF induce PGE2 in hypothalamus → raised set-point → fever.
Vasoconstriction → mottling, prolonged CRT → early shock.
Signs: Grunting, RR >60, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, petechiae, lethargy.
Tachycardia out of proportion to fever → shock.
Dx: CRP peaks at 36-48 hours (early CRP may reassure falsely); procalcitonin rises within 2-4 hours, more bacterial-specific.
Normal CSF WBC <5/µL; bacterial meningitis → low glucose.
Rx: Blood cultures before antibiotics; number of cultures and volume of blood decide sensitivity.
Infant <3 months ≥ 38 °C → full septic screen.
Shocked child: cultures → antibiotics within the hour; never delay for LP.

Def: Choose by bug (age, site), penetration, severity, local resistance; culture first.
Review antibiotic therapy at 48-72 hours to narrow or stop.
Cause: Neonate: GBS, E. coli, Listeria. Older: pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib.
Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins, so neonatal cover needs amoxicillin.
Patho: β -lactams inhibit penicillin-binding protein transpeptidases; β -lactamase hydrolyzes the β -lactam ring.
Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent killing; β -lactams show time-dependent killing.
Signs: Chloramphenicol → gray baby syndrome; tetracyclines → permanent tooth staining.
Ceftriaxone in neonates displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium.
Aminoglycosides: acute tubular necrosis, ototoxicity; fluoroquinolones: tendon rupture, cartilage damage.
Dx: Blood culture before first dose → review at 48-72 hours.
Narrow to culture, IV → oral when afebrile, shortest effective duration.
Rx: Neonatal sepsis: ampicillin + gentamicin; suspected meningitis: ampicillin + cefotaxime. Beyond neonate: ceftriaxone.
CAP: oral amoxicillin; MSSA: nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin; newborn gonorrhea: ceftriaxone.
No antibiotics for colds, bronchiolitis, viral wheeze.

Def: Lyme: spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, Ixodes tick (Europe: Ixodes ricinus). Mumps = paramyxovirus parotitis.
Cause: Lyme: Northeast and upper Midwest US; needs >24-36 h attachment. Mumps: incubation 16-18 days.
Patho: Spirochetes spread centrifugally → expanding erythema with central clearing.
Mumps: viraemia seeds glands + CNS → explains every complication.
Signs: Lyme stage 2: facial palsy, meningitis, carditis (AV block); stage 3: encephalopathy, arthritis.
Mumps: painful parotid swelling; orchitis in post-pubertal males; meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness.
Dx: Erythema migrans is clinical: tick bite + growing erythema more than 5 cm; no serology.
Early disseminated/late: ELISA then Western if confirmation needed. Mumps: raised amylase, RT-PCR/IgM.
Rx: Erythema migrans: young child amoxicillin; older doxycycline (US any age, 10 days).
Neuro/high-grade block: IV ceftriaxone. Prophylaxis if tick attached ≥36 hours, within 72 hours.
Mumps: supportive; MMR ×2.

topics.title: Clinical manifestations of Epstein-Barr virus infection.

Def: Infectious mononucleosis (“kissing disease”) is caused by EBV (HHV-4): fever, pharyngitis, nodes, splenomegaly.
Cause: Most common in teenagers; spread by saliva or respiratory secretions; young children mild or silent.
EBV: Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Patho: EBV first infects oropharyngeal epithelium, then B cells via CD21.
Reactive CD8 T cells = Downey type II atypical lymphocytes.
Polyclonal B activation → heterophile antibodies.
Signs: Fatigue, fever, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, hepatosplenomegaly; grey-white tonsillar exudate.
Raised LFTs (hepatitis) and lymphocytosis.
Amoxicillin in EBV causes a maculopapular rash - not true penicillin allergy.
Dx: Atypical lymphocytes >10% on smear; Monospot often negative under 4-5 years → VCA IgM.
Cytopenias or blasts → exclude leukaemia.
Rx: Supportive: rest, fluids, paracetamol (acetaminophen); aciclovir useless.
Steroids only for airway obstruction, haemolysis or thrombocytopenia.
No contact sport for 3-4 weeks because of splenic rupture.

Def: Measles (Paramyxoviridae), rubella (togavirus), scarlet fever (group A strep exotoxin).
Cause: Measles most contagious (R0 12-18), aerosol; scarlet fever 2-10 years; rubella in first trimester → congenital rubella.
Patho: Measles kills memory cells → immune amnesia; rubella crosses placenta → organogenesis damage.
GAS pyrogenic exotoxins = superantigens → capillary dilation.
Signs: Measles: 3 Cs + Koplik spots → rash day 3-4, ears downward.
Rubella: postauricular and suboccipital nodes; CRS: cataract, sensorineural deafness, PDA (80% foetal injury).
Scarlet: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, desquamation.
Dx: Measles pneumonia is the commonest death; SSPE years later.
Scarlet: throat swab; Rapid Strep has low sensitivity, culture confirms; ASO later.
Rx: Measles: supportive + vitamin A; contacts MMR ≤ 72 h or Ig ≤ 6 days.
Scarlet fever: phenoxymethylpenicillin 10 days (US also amoxicillin) → prevents rheumatic fever.
Prevent: MMR ×2; avoid if pregnant or immunocompromised.

Def: Worms (helminths) and single-cell parasites (protozoa) in children.
Cause: Enterobius (commonest Europe), Ascaris, Toxocara (puppies), Giardia, Entamoeba, Toxoplasma, malaria.
Giardia is fecal-oral (daycare, camping streams); Cryptosporidium in HIV/AIDS.
Patho: Tissue-migrating worms → Th2 / IL-5 → eosinophilia.
Giardia flattens villi → fat/lactose malabsorption; Entamoeba trophozoites invade colon.
Signs: Threadworm: nocturnal perianal itch. Toxocara: leukocoria (ocular larva migrans), mimics retinoblastoma.
Giardia: bloating, foul-smelling floating, fatty stools.
Entamoeba: bloody diarrhea, right lobe liver abscess.
Congenital toxo: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications. Malaria: fever, anemia, splenomegaly.
Dx: Sticky tape (scotch tape) test; Giardia: trophozoites or cysts in stool.
Entamoeba: trophozoites with endocytosed RBCs; biopsy with flask-shaped lesions.
Fever after endemic travel = malaria → urgent thick/thin films.
Rx: Threadworm: mebendazole, repeat after 2 weeks, treat the whole household.
Giardia/Entamoeba: metronidazole (or tinidazole); Toxocara: albendazole.
Congenital toxo: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folate (leucovorin) for 12 months.

topics.title: Clinical manifestations of Herpes simplex virus, Parvovirus, Coxsackie virus infection.

Def: HSV (vesicles, latency), parvovirus B19 (single-stranded DNA, fifth disease), Coxsackie (enterovirus).
Cause: HSV: direct contact; neonatal from genital tract lesions.
Enteroviruses faecal-oral, summer/autumn.
Patho: HSV stays latent in sensory ganglia (HSV-1: trigeminal ganglion) → recurrence.
B19 infects erythroid progenitors via P antigen → aplastic crisis in sickle cell or spherocytosis.
Signs: HSV: herpes labialis, dendritic corneal ulcers; eczema herpeticum = punched-out erosions + fever.
B19: slapped cheek, lacy rash; fetal hydrops fetalis.
Coxsackie A: hand, foot and mouth disease; B: myocarditis, Bornholm disease.
Dx: HSV encephalitis: temporal lobe, CSF HSV PCR, MRI; Tzanck smear also detects HSV.
Aplastic crisis: falling Hb + reticulocytopenia.
Pregnant, B19 antibody positive: reassurance; >20 weeks weekly ultrasounds.
Rx: Suspected HSV encephalitis → IV aciclovir immediately; eczema herpeticum: aciclovir.
Neonatal HSV: high-dose IV aciclovir 14-21 days; genital HSV in labor: cesarean delivery.
Aplastic crisis: transfusion; fetal anemia → intrauterine RBC transfusion.

Def: Varicella (chickenpox) = primary VZV; herpes zoster = its reactivation, unilateral dermatomal rash.
Cause: Airborne; incubation 10-21 days; infectious 1-2 days before rash until all lesions crusted.
Patho: Repeated viraemia waves → crops: lesions in different stages of healing together.
VZV becomes latent in dorsal root (sensory) ganglia → falling T-cell immunity → zoster.
Signs: Itchy centripetal rash (trunk first), headache, fever. Zoster: painful, does not cross midline.
Fever returning after day 3-4 → invasive group A streptococcus. Hutchinson sign → eye.
Dx: Clinical (Tzanck smear). Maternal varicella before 20 weeks → congenital varicella syndrome.
Maternal rash -5 to +2 days of delivery → severe neonatal varicella.
Rx: Paracetamol, emollients; avoid ibuprofen, never aspirin (Reye).
Aciclovir for neonates, immunocompromised, severe disease (IV if disseminated); VZIG for high-risk contacts.
Live attenuated vaccine: 2 doses (1 and 4 y); post-zoster neuralgia: TCAs, gabapentin.

Def: Bacterial, viral, fungal skin infections; depth decides the picture.
Cause: S. aureus and GAS via breaks (eczema, bites, varicella); tinea capitis in young African American children.
Patho: S. aureus exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 in the granular layer → bullous impetigo, SSSS.
Necrotising fasciitis thromboses perforators → deep death, mild skin.
Signs: Impetigo: honey-coloured (golden) crusts, well. Erysipelas: upper dermis, sharp raised edge; cellulitis ill-defined.
SSSS: Nikolsky +, spares mucous membranes (desmoglein-3) -unlike TEN.
Necrotising fasciitis: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, shock.
Dx: Proptosis/painful eye movement → orbital cellulitis → CT.
SSSS blister fluid sterile → culture the focus. Tinea: Wood lamp for Microsporum; scabies: papules and burrows.
Rx: Impetigo: topical (mupirocin), or oral flucloxacillin (US cephalexin) if widespread/bullous.
SSSS/orbital: admit, IV antibiotics. Abscess: incision and drainage. Tinea capitis: oral antifungal.
Necrotising fasciitis: urgent surgery + clindamycin, consider IVIG.

topics.title: Staphylococcus aureus infections. Toxic shock syndrome

Def: S. aureus: pyogenic invasive disease; TSS = superantigen cytokine storm.
Cause: Nasal carriage ~1/3. TSS: tampons, retained gauze, burns, wounds, nasal packing, varicella lesions.
Most common cause of osteomyelitis.
Patho: Coagulase builds a fibrin wall → abscesses, furuncles, carbuncles.
TSST-1 superantigen binds MHC II and TCR V β → T-cell activation (up to 20%).
MRSA alters penicillin-binding proteins; S. aureus makes β -lactamase.
Signs: TSS: high fever, erythroderma, hypotension, multi-organ failure.
Desquamation of palms/soles 1-2 weeks later.
Food poisoning: vomiting 1-6 hours after eating (preformed enterotoxin).
Dx: Bacteraemia → search bone, joint, heart focus + repeat cultures.
Staph TSS blood culture usually negative; strep TSS positive (toxic shock-like syndrome: GAS).
Rx: TSS: fluids, vasopressors, source removal; β -lactam + clindamycin (suppresses toxin synthesis); IVIG if severe.
MSSA: anti-staph penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin), cefazolin; drain pus.
MRSA → vancomycin, linezolid; daptomycin for bacteremia; ceftaroline binds altered PBPs.

Def: Toxin diseases of C. tetani (spastic paralysis) and C. botulinum (flaccid paralysis).
Cause: Tetanus: spores in soil/rusty nails, deep wounds, unclean cord with poorly immunized mother.
Infant botulism: ingested spores from honey or juice (or inhaled dust) in immature gut.
Patho: Tetanospasmin → retrograde axonal transport → blocks GABA/glycine release → spasms.
Botulinum cleaves SNARE → no acetylcholine release → flaccid + autonomic block.
Signs: Tetanus: jaw first - trismus (lock jaw), risus sardonicus, spasms, opisthotonus; conscious. Neonate stops sucking.
Botulism: constipation, early diplopia, ptosis, descending symmetric flaccid paralysis, floppy head; afebrile, alert.
Dx: Tetanus: clinical assessment only; toxin effects, consciousness and sensation preserved.
Rx: Tetanus: human tetanus immune globulin (HTIG), debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines, ICU.
Prevent: maternal toxoid vaccination; vaccinate after recovery (no immunity after tetanus).
Infant botulism: supportive + human-derived botulism immune globulin; adults: horse-derived antitoxin; no aminoglycosides.

Def: Osteomyelitis (bone) and septic arthritis (joint) - bacterial, septic arthritis a surgical emergency.
Cause: S. aureus most common; Kingella kingae 6 months-4 years; GBS/E. coli neonates.
Salmonella in sickle cell; Pseudomonas after nail puncture.
Patho: Children: hematogenous spread; bacteria settle in the metaphysis (slow flow in sinusoids) → pus → sequestrum, involucrum.
Under 18 months, transphyseal vessels spread infection to the joint.
Signs: Fever, hot swollen joint, won't bear weight; pseudoparalysis in infants.
Septic hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated.
Dx: Blood culture, CRP, ESR; ultrasound effusion; X-ray normal for 10-14 days.
Joint aspiration: Gram stain, culture, PCR.
MRI best for osteomyelitis (high ESR, normal X-ray → MRI).
Rx: MSSA: nafcillin, oxacillin, dicloxacillin, IV cefazolin; clindamycin or vancomycin if MRSA.
Short IV (2-4 days) → oral; about 3 weeks total.
Septic arthritis: joint washout; drain subperiosteal abscess, remove sequestrum.

Def: Congenital disorders: DDH, clubfoot, osteogenesis imperfecta, achondroplasia.
Cause: DDH: breech, family history, female sex, first-born, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling.
OI: COL1A1/COL1A2 (usually AD); achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain-of-function, older fathers.
Patho: Femoral head displaced → acetabulum fails to mould → DDH.
OI: defective type I collagen → fragile bone, blue sclerae.
FGFR3 overactive → poor endochondral growth → rhizomelic limbs.
Signs: DDH: Barlow/Ortolani positive; later limited abduction, leg-length discrepancy.
Clubfoot: rigid cavus, adductus, varus, equinus; OI: low-trauma fractures.
Achondroplasia: macrocephaly, trident hands, foramen magnum stenosis.
Dx: Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip; Barlow dislocates a located one.
Hip ultrasound before about 4.5 months; X-ray afterwards.
Consider OI in non-accidental injury. Scoliosis: forward bend test → X-ray.
Rx: DDH: Pavlik harness under 6 months → closed → open reduction.
Clubfoot: Ponseti casting → Achilles tenotomy → bracing. OI: IV bisphosphonates.
Scoliosis Cobb 10-30°: monitor; 30-40°: brace; >40-50°: surgery.

Def: JIA: arthritis of unknown cause, onset before 16, lasting at least 6 weeks.
Cause: Subtypes: oligoarticular (~50%, young ANA+ girls), polyarticular RF-/RF+, systemic, enthesitis-related (HLA-B27), psoriatic.
Patho: T cells + TNF- α, IL-1, IL-6 → synovial hyperplasia (pannus) → erosion.
Systemic JIA: IL-1 and IL-6 driven; ANA and RF negative.
MAS: failed cytotoxic killing → cytokine storm; ESR falls as fibrinogen is consumed.
Signs: Swollen joint, morning stiffness; limb overgrowth.
Oligoarticular ANA-positive: silent anterior uveitis (iritis), painless white eye.
Systemic: quotidian fever, salmon-pink macular rash, hepatosplenomegaly, serositis.
Dx: Clinical; ANA → uveitis risk; RF/anti-CCP → erosive course.
Exclude leukaemia (night pain, cytopenia, LDH) and septic arthritis.
ANA+ oligoarticular: slit lamp every 3 months. MAS: huge ferritin, falling ESR.
Rx: NSAIDs → intra-articular triamcinolone → methotrexate once weekly + folic acid.
Biologics: anti-TNF, abatacept, tocilizumab; sJIA: anakinra/tocilizumab first-line.
MAS (most serious complication): IV methylprednisolone, anakinra, ciclosporin.

topics.title: Causes, diagnostic and treatment of acute viral hepatitis

Def: Acute inflammation of the liver from hepatotropic viruses A-E.
Cause: A, E: faecal-oral, self-limiting; B, C, D: blood/vertical, can become chronic.
Others: EBV, CMV, HSV, paracetamol, autoimmune, Wilson.
Patho: Cytotoxic T cells kill hepatocytes → ALT/AST in thousands; zone I first.
Impaired bilirubin handling → jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch.
Perinatal HBV becomes chronic in about 90% (vs ~5% adults).
Signs: Prodrome: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting → then jaundice; HAV in young children mostly anicteric.
Dx: IgM anti-HAV; HBsAg + IgM anti-HBc = acute B; anti-HCV + HCV RNA.
HBeAg predicts infectivity; severity by INR (not corrected by vitamin K), glucose, mental state.
PALF: INR ≥ 1.5 with encephalopathy, or ≥ 2.0 without.
Rx: Supportive: fluids, avoid hepatotoxins; admit if INR raised, hypoglycaemic, encephalopathic.
Chronic only: HBV entecavir/tenofovir; HCV DAAs.
Newborn of HBsAg+ mother: HBV vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours.

Def: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection; childhood TB = recent infection from an adult contact.
Cause: Droplet nuclei from adult with cavitary pulmonary TB.
Risk: age under 2, HIV, malnutrition, measles.
Patho: Hilar nodes → Ghon complex = peripheral lung focus + hilar nodes.
Cord factor → TNF- α → granulomas.
Under 2 years: blood spread → miliary TB and meningitis.
Signs: Primary TB mostly asymptomatic; cough >2 weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss.
Scrofula, Pott disease, erythema nodosum.
Dx: Contact + TST/IGRA + CXR; IGRA has fewer BCG false positives.
PPD positive: ≥ 5 mm high risk, ≥ 10 intermediate, ≥ 15 low risk.
Early-morning gastric aspirates or induced sputum → Xpert MTB/RIF, culture. Meningitis: lymphocytes, high protein, very low glucose.
Rx: RIPE: 2 months HRZ(E) → 4 months HR (rifampin, isoniazid); pyridoxine with isoniazid.
TB meningitis: 12 months + corticosteroids.
Contacts under 5 → preventive therapy even if tests negative.

topics.title: Disorders of the humoral immune system

Def: Primary antibody (B-cell) deficiencies: XLA, CVID, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgM.
Cause: XLA: BTK mutation, boys; CVID: no B-cell differentiation into plasma cells.
Hyper-IgM: mutated CD40L on Th cells. Secondary: nephrotic syndrome, rituximab, malignancy.
Patho: XLA: no B-cell maturation → no opsonising IgG → encapsulated bacteria escape phagocytosis.
Maternal IgG wanes → onset after ~6 months; hyper-IgM: defective class switching.
Signs: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections → bronchiectasis; enteroviral meningoencephalitis.
XLA: absent tonsils and nodes; CVID: autoimmunity, lymphoma.
IgA deficiency (most common): mostly asymptomatic; transfusion anaphylaxis.
Dx: Quantitative IgG, IgA, IgM; IgA deficiency: normal IgG and IgM.
Vaccine responses (tetanus, Hib, pneumococcal) before and 4-6 weeks after booster.
Flow cytometry: B cells (CD19) absent in XLA; genetics (BTK).
Rx: Immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG) every 3-4 weeks or subcutaneous weekly.
Prompt antibiotics; no live vaccines in XLA.
IgA deficiency: usually none; washed blood products.

Def: T-cell defects - almost always combined (antibody fails too): SCID, DiGeorge, Wiskott-Aldrich.
Cause: SCID: X-linked common γ -chain (IL2RG) commonest, ADA deficiency, RAG mutations.
DiGeorge: 22q11.2 deletion; WAS: X-linked WAS protein; secondary: HIV, steroids.
Patho: No T cells → no control of viruses, fungi, intracellular opportunists; no B-cell help.
ADA deficiency: dATP toxic to lymphocytes; RAG → VDJ recombination defects.
DiGeorge: abnormal 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic + parathyroid hypoplasia.
Signs: First months: thrush, Pneumocystis, chronic viral diarrhoea, failure to thrive.
DiGeorge: hypocalcaemia, conotruncal heart defects, cleft palate.
WAS triad: eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, infections.
Dx: Lymphopenia, absent thymic shadow; absent T cells on flow cytometry.
Newborn screening: TRECs. DiGeorge: calcium, PTH, echo, FISH for 22q11.2.
Rx: Isolation; no live vaccines; only irradiated, CMV-negative blood.
