TMP-SMX (co-trimoxazole) PJP prophylaxis, antifungals, immunoglobulin replacement.
Cure: stem cell transplant (>90% if <3.5 months); ADA: pegademase, gene therapy.

topics.title: Role of the complement system and diseases of the complement system

Def: Complement: three pathways (classical begins C1, alternative C3) converging on C3 → opsonise, recruit, lyse.
Cause: Inherited deficiency of early classical (C1q, C2, C4), C3, terminal (C5-C9), properdin, factor H/I.
C1-inhibitor deficiency (AD) → hereditary angioedema.
Patho: Early classical deficiency → SLE-like; C3 → encapsulated bacteria.
C5-C9/properdin deficiency → no MAC → recurrent Neisseria infection.
No C1-inhibitor → bradykinin excess → vascular leak.
Signs: Lupus-like disease; severe pyogenic infections; recurrent meningococcal disease.
Factor H defect → atypical HUS.
HAE: non-itchy swelling of face, gut, larynx; no urticaria.
Dx: CH50 (classical), AH50 (alternative), C3, C4 levels.
Second or unusual-serogroup meningococcal episode → complement screen.
HAE screening test: low C4 → C1-inhibitor level and function.
Rx: Vaccinate: meningococcus ACWY + B, pneumococcus, Hib; early antibiotics for fever.
aHUS: eculizumab (anti-C5) - requires meningococcal vaccination.
HAE: C1-inhibitor concentrate or icatibant -adrenaline/antihistamines/steroids don't work.

Def: HIV infects CD4 T cells; in children mainly vertical, most intrapartum.
Cause: Transmission: in utero, intrapartum, breastfeeding; adolescents sexual or drug use.
Patho: gp120 binds CD4 + CCR5 (macrophages, early) or CXCR4 (T cells, late); gp41 mediates fusion.
→ CD4 depletion and immune activation.
Developing thymus, higher viral set points → faster progression than adults.
Signs: Failure to thrive, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, parotid swelling, chronic diarrhoea.
Persistent candidiasis, LIP, encephalopathy; infant 3-6 months with severe hypoxia → PJP.
Dx: Under 18 months: HIV DNA/RNA PCR because maternal IgG persists.
Over 18 months: antibody/antigen tests as in adults.
Rx: Prevent: maternal ART, neonatal zidovudine, avoid breastfeeding → transmission <1%.
ART at diagnosis, regardless of CD4: 2 NRTIs + dolutegravir.
Co-trimoxazole from 4-6 weeks against PJP; avoid BCG; rifabutin replaces rifampin with protease inhibitors.

Def: Infections by organisms harmless to healthy hosts; the immune defect predicts the organism.
Cause: HIV/AIDS, high-dose immunosuppression (transplant), steroids; chemotherapy neutropenia, CGD.
Antibody, complement, asplenia (XLA, CVID, sickle cell).
Patho: No neutrophils → Pseudomonas, S. aureus, Candida, Aspergillus.
No T cells → Pneumocystis, CMV, Cryptococcus, MAC.
No antibody/spleen → encapsulated bacteria.
Signs: Febrile neutropenia: fever may be the only sign of sepsis.
PJP: fever, dry cough, hypoxia, high LDH; MAC: high fever, watery diarrhea.
CMV: retinitis, colitis; Cryptococcus: fungal meningitis.
Dx: Febrile neutropenia = ≥38°C + neutrophils <0.5 × 10⁹/L; cultures line + periphery.
PJP: bronchoalveolar lavage; CMV retinitis: CD4 ≤ 50, cotton wool spots.
Rx: Piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour; add vancomycin for line/instability.
PJP: TMP-SMX + steroids if PaO2 ≤ 70 mmHg; MAC: clarithromycin + ethambutol.
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine & sulfadiazine; varicella: IV aciclovir.

Def: Non-suppurative sequelae of GAS: acute rheumatic fever and PSGN.
Cause: ARF: GAS pharyngitis 2-4 weeks before.
PSGN: pharyngitis 1-2 weeks or skin 3-6 weeks before.
Patho: ARF: M protein cross-reacts with self-antigens (molecular mimicry); type II HSR.
PSGN: immune complexes → complement → low C3 → ↓GFR → salt retention.
Signs: ARF (J♥NES): migratory polyarthritis, carditis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea.
Mitral valve most common: acute regurgitation; chronic fish-mouth stenosis.
PSGN: cola urine, periorbital oedema, hypertension, oliguria.
Dx: Jones: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, + evidence of GAS (ASO/anti-DNase B).
Histology: Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells; echo for subclinical carditis.
PSGN: low C3, normal C4, normalising within 8 weeks.
Rx: ARF: penicillin V 10 days (anaphylaxis: macrolides); aspirin/naproxen for arthritis.
Secondary prophylaxis: benzathine penicillin IM every 3-4 weeks.
PSGN: supportive; strep-throat antibiotics prevent ARF, not PSGN.

Def: Pertussis: toxin-mediated Bordetella pertussis respiratory infection (whooping cough).
Cause: Aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus, spread by respiratory droplets; attack rate >80%.
Adolescents/adults often the source.
Patho: Filamentous hemagglutinin attaches; tracheal toxin kills ciliated cells → violent coughing.
Pertussis toxin disables Gi → ↑cAMP → lymphocytosis, hypoglycaemia.
Lymphocytes >30 × 10⁹/L → leukostasis → pulmonary hypertension.
Signs: Catarrhal (most infectious) → paroxysmal: whoop, post-tussive vomiting → convalescent.
Infants <6 months: apnoea and cyanosis, often no whoop; pneumothorax risk.
Dx: PCR of nasopharyngeal swab early; culture on Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou agar.
FBC: marked lymphocytosis.
Rx: Early macrolides (azithromycin), also in neonates (erythromycin: pyloric stenosis).
Admit infants <6 months with apnoea/cyanosis; prophylactic macrolides for all close contacts.
Prevent: Tdap in pregnancy + DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months.

Def: Non-typhoidal salmonella enterocolitis and typhoid (enteric) fever.
Cause: NTS: raw chicken/eggs, unpasteurised milk, reptiles (turtles); large infective dose.
Typhoid: S. Typhi/Paratyphi, humans the only reservoir; travel to endemic areas.
Patho: Gram-negative, non-lactose fermenting, H₂ S-positive rod with type III secretion system.
Typhoid: Peyer patches → macrophages → bacteraemia; necrosis → perforation in week 3.
Signs: NTS: inflammatory diarrhea with leukocytes; sickle cell → osteomyelitis.
Typhoid: abdominal pain, stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots.
Dx: NTS: stool culture.
Typhoid: blood culture in week 1 (bone marrow most sensitive); leucopenia typical.
Rx: NTS low-risk: supportive care; antibiotics prolong faecal carriage.
Antibiotics only if <3 months, immunocompromised, sickle cell, invasive (sickle cell sepsis: ceftriaxone).
Typhoid: ceftriaxone or azithromycin; carbapenem for XDR; vaccine.

Def: Influenza A/B: orthomyxovirus; drift → epidemics, shift (reassortment) → pandemics.
Cause: Respiratory droplets; children main spreaders.
High risk: under 5, chronic lung/heart/neuro disease, immunosuppression, aspirin therapy.
Patho: Drift = point mutations in hemagglutinin or neuraminidase; HA binds sialic acid, NA cleaves it.
Ciliated cells destroyed → cytokines; denuded airway → secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Signs: Abrupt fever, myalgia, dry cough; infants mimic sepsis, febrile seizures.
Influenza B: calf myositis; associated with Guillain-Barré; better then worse → pneumonia.
Dx: Clinical in season; PCR on nasopharyngeal swab for hospitalised/high-risk.
Rx: Supportive: paracetamol/ibuprofen; no aspirin (Reye syndrome).
Oseltamivir (neuraminidase inhibitor) for high-risk/severe, ideally within 48 hours.
Annual vaccine from 6 months; first time under 9 years: two doses 4 weeks apart.

topics.title: Routine management of the healthy newborn infant. Disorders of the newborn adaptation.

Def: Care of the healthy newborn and disorders of the transition to extrauterine life.
Cause: Adaptation disorders: TTN, PPHN, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, jaundice.
Hypoglycaemia risk: infants of diabetic mothers, small, preterm, cold, asphyxiated.
Patho: Labour catecholamines → ENaC clears lung fluid → aeration; TTN = delayed clearance.
Brown fat (uncoupling protein 1) gives non-shivering heat.
Signs: TTN: term baby after C-section with grunting; hypoglycaemia mnemonic JOLTS.
Jaundice within 24 h is always pathological; cephalohematoma does not cross sutures.
Dx: Apgar 1, 5, 10 minutes; examination within 72 h.
Screening: pulse oximetry, hearing, heel-prick blood spot.
Pre-/post-ductal saturation gap → PPHN.
Rx: Dry and stimulate; delay cord clamping ≥60 s; skin-to-skin; breastfeed.
Vitamin K 1 mg IM; HBV vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours if mother HBsAg-positive.
Hypoglycaemia: feed, dextrose gel, IV dextrose; jaundice: phototherapy; TTN: supportive.

Def: RDS: surfactant deficiency in the preterm lung (mature levels around week 35).
Cause: Prematurity (most important), maternal diabetes (fetal insulin), caesarean delivery.
Patho: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; none → alveoli collapse (Laplace, P = 2T/r) → hypoxaemia.
Prematurity → inadequate surfactant → alveoli fail to open → poor oxygenation.
Signs: Within 4 h of birth: tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, recession, cyanosis.
Dx: CXR: ground-glass with air bronchograms, atelectasis, low lung volumes (BAD).
Mature lung: L:S ratio ≥ 2.
Rx: Prevent: maternal antenatal glucocorticoids.
CPAP from birth → artificial surfactant if FiO₂ >0.30.
Caffeine for apnoea; antibiotics until GBS excluded; complications: NEC, ROP, BPD.

Def: MAS: respiratory distress from meconium aspiration in term and post-term infants.
Cause: Post-term (postmaturity), growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, oligohydramnios, abnormal CTG.
Meconium in a preterm → think Listeria.
Patho: Fetal hypoxia → increased peristalsis and anal sphincter relaxation → meconium passage → aspiration.
Ball-valve air trapping → pneumothorax; meconium inactivates surfactant; PPHN.
Signs: Meconium-stained skin/nails/cord; distress from birth; barrel chest, crackles.
Air leak (pneumothorax) in 10-20%.
Dx: CXR: coarse patchy infiltrates + hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms.
Pre-/post-ductal saturation gap → PPHN.
Rx: Non-vigorous baby: no routine tracheal suctioning; start ventilation within the first minute.
NICU: oxygen, CPAP/ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide for PPHN.
ECMO if refractory; antibiotics until sepsis excluded.

topics.title: Primary Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)

Def: PPHN: pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall after birth.
Right-to-left shunt at the PDA and foramen ovale.
Cause: Commonest: meconium aspiration; also sepsis, asphyxia, RDS.
Maternal SSRIs or NSAIDs in pregnancy; diaphragmatic hernia.
Patho: Shunted blood bypasses alveoli → FiO₂ barely helps.
Hypoxia + acidosis → more vasoconstriction → vicious circle.
Signs: Term baby, cyanosis out of proportion to lung disease, labile saturations.
Loud single S2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur.
Dx: Pre-post-ductal gap (>3%); pre-ductal = right hand.
Echocardiography confirms the shunt and excludes cyanotic heart disease (TAPVD).
Rx: Minimal handling, sedation, normothermia; oxygen, avoid hyperoxia; surfactant.
Inhaled nitric oxide 20 ppm if OI >20-25 (relaxes vessels via cGMP).
Support BP (milrinone, adrenaline, vasopressin); ECMO if refractory.

Def: Infections passed mother → baby transplacentally, intrapartum or postnatally.
Cause: Transplacental: TORCH, parvovirus B19, VZV, Zika.
Intrapartum: GBS, E. coli, HSV, HBV, HIV, gonococcus, chlamydia.
Postnatal: NICU lines/hands (CoNS, Staph aureus, Candida), breast milk, contacts.
Patho: Early pregnancy → organogenesis hit → malformation; later → active disease at birth.
Parvovirus B19 → fetal anaemia and hydrops; HBV in infants → up to 90% carriers.
Signs: Neonatal HSV: seizures, vesicles, hepatitis.
Gonococcal conjunctivitis 2-5 days; chlamydial 5-14 days; silver nitrate: chemical conjunctivitis.
Dx: Antenatal screening: HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis; maternal GBS status.
Rx: HBV: vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours (at latest 24 h); breastfeeding allowed.
HSV → IV aciclovir; gonococcus → ceftriaxone; chlamydia → azithromycin; GBS → penicillin G prophylaxis.
HIV → ART, no breastfeeding; peripartum chickenpox → VZIG; no fetal scalp electrodes in HIV/HCV.

Def: Congenital Toxoplasma, Other (syphilis, VZV, parvovirus, Zika), Rubella, CMV, HSV.
Cause: Maternal infection crossing the placenta (transplacental); CMV is the commonest; highest risk 1st trimester.
Patho: Cross placenta → attack dividing fetal cells → IUGR, CNS and eye damage.
Parvovirus B19 → hydrops fetalis; VZV → congenital varicella syndrome (limb hypoplasia).
Signs: CMV: blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, periventricular calcification, hearing loss.
Toxo: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, diffuse calcification; rubella: cataract, deafness, PDA.
Syphilis: snuffles, desquamating rash, saber shins.
Dx: CMV: urine/saliva PCR within 21 days; 80-90% asymptomatic at birth → hearing and eye follow-up.
Toxoplasmosis: antibody testing.
Rx: Symptomatic CMV: valganciclovir 6 months; toxo: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folate.
Syphilis: penicillin G; VZV: VZIG; rubella prevented by MMR.
HSV lesions in labour: C-section; acyclovir from 36 weeks.

topics.title: Neonatal and late onset neonatal sepsis

Def: Early-onset (<72 hours) = vertical; late-onset (>72 h) = nosocomial/community.
Cause: Early: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; risks: prolonged ROM, chorioamnionitis, prematurity.
Late: coagulase-negative staphylococci (lines), Staph aureus, Gram-negatives, Candida.
Patho: Small neutrophil reserve, low complement/Ig + lines breaching skin → rapid spread.
Signs: Subtle: apnoea, temperature instability, grunting, poor feeding, mottling.
Dx: Blood culture, serial CRP, lumbar puncture.
GBS identified by maternal vaginal screening.
Rx: Prevention: intrapartum penicillin G at least 4 hours before delivery; not late-onset GBS.
Without meningitis: ampicillin + gentamicin within 1 hour; with meningitis: ampicillin + cefotaxime.
Prior invasive GBS baby → prophylaxis in every subsequent pregnancy.

topics.title: Central nervous system disorders of the neonates

Def: Preterm: IVH and PVL; term: HIE, stroke, infection, kernicterus, birth trauma.
Cause: IVH: preterm <32 weeks, within 72 hours; HIE = commonest seizure cause.
Subgaleal haemorrhage after vacuum delivery; Erb palsy: lateral traction at delivery.
Patho: IVH: fragile germinal matrix bleeds → hydrocephalus.
Watershed white matter ischaemia → PVL → spastic diplegia.
Signs: Neonatal seizures are subtle; IVH: low tone, seizures, rapidly increasing head circumference.
Scalp swelling crossing sutures + shock → subgaleal haemorrhage; Erb palsy: waiter's tip.
Dx: Cranial ultrasound; Papile I-IV; grade IV = periventricular haemorrhagic infarction.
Seizures: check glucose and calcium first, then sodium, magnesium, infection; EEG.
Rx: Seizures: phenobarbital first line.
IVH prevention: antenatal steroids, magnesium, delayed cord clamping; avoid pressure/CO2 swings.
Erb/Klumpke palsy: spontaneous resolution within 3 months (80%).

topics.title: Skin and umbilical disorders of the neonates

Def: Benign newborn rashes, vascular lesions, skin infections and umbilical problems.
Cause: Benign: erythema toxicum, milia, miliaria, nevus simplex, dermal melanocytosis.
Infective: bullous impetigo/SSSS, candida, HSV, omphalitis.
Patho: SSSS: exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein-1 → mucosa spared.
Omphalitis → umbilical vein → sepsis, portal vein thrombosis.
Signs: Erythema toxicum: sterile pustules full of eosinophils; miliaria: sweat-duct blockage with heat.
Strawberry hemangioma grows rapidly then regresses; umbilical hernia soft, reducible.
Urine at navel = patent urachus; faeces = vitelline duct; granuloma: soft, moist, pink.
Dx: Cord separates at 5-15 days; delayed + neutrophilia → leukocyte adhesion deficiency (CD18).
Single umbilical artery → congenital and chromosomal anomalies.
Rx: Benign rashes → reassurance; hemangioma → propranolol if eye, airway, ulcer.
Granuloma → silver nitrate; umbilical hernia: monitor, resolves by age 5.
SSSS → IV flucloxacillin; omphalitis → IV antibiotics; HSV → aciclovir.

Def: NEC: ischaemic-inflammatory bowel necrosis in preterms after feeds start.
Meconium ileus: terminal ileum blocked by sticky meconium = cystic fibrosis (~15%).
Cause: NEC: prematurity (biggest risk factor), formula feeding, abnormal flora, poor mucosal perfusion; breast milk protective.
Patho: Immature barrier + abnormal flora + poor perfusion (e.g.
hypoxaemia) → bacteria invade wall → pneumatosis.
Signs: NEC: abdominal distension, nutritional intolerance, bloody stool; instability, low platelets, acidosis.
Meconium ileus: distension, bilious vomiting, no meconium.
Dx: NEC X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas; Rigler sign = perforation.
Baby cannot be moved: horizontal X-ray from side position, lying on back.
Meconium ileus: soap-bubble, microcolon; later sweat test.
Rx: NEC: NPO (bowel rest), NG decompression, IV fluids, TPN, IV antibiotics (gram-negative, anaerobes).
Surgery for perforation, peritonitis, or worsening despite medical therapy.
Meconium ileus: Gastrografin enema → surgery if it fails.

Def: CDH: usually left-sided posterolateral Bochdalek hernia.
OA: proximal blind pouch, usually with distal TEF (85%).
Cause: CDH: abdominal viscera herniate into chest; OA/TEF: associated VACTERL anomalies (mesodermal defects).
Patho: CDH: pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension determine survival.
OA: fetus can't swallow → polyhydramnios; saliva pools → choking, aspiration.
Signs: CDH: respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, heart sounds on right.
OA: excess drooling, choking at first feeding; distal fistula: abdominal distension.
Cough since birth, always during feeding → H-type TEF.
Dx: OA: firm NG tube coils in pouch on X-ray; gastric gas = distal fistula.
Pure OA: gasless abdomen; VACTERL screen, echo.
Rx: CDH: intubate, no bag-mask, NG tube, gentle ventilation, treat pulmonary hypertension.
CDH surgery after stabilisation: physiological, not surgical, emergency.
OA/TEF: surgery after Replogle tube; look for VACTERL.

topics.title: Duodenal stenosis, bowel atresia, omphalocele, gastroschisis

Def: Congenital gut obstructions (duodenal, jejunoileal, anal atresia) and abdominal wall defects.
Cause: Duodenal: failed recanalisation, trisomy 21; jejunoileal: in-utero vascular accident.
Omphalocele: Beckwith-Wiedemann, trisomies 13, 18; gastroschisis: young mothers.
Patho: Obstruction below ampulla → bilious vomiting from first feed, polyhydramnios.
Signs: Duodenal: bilious vomiting, flat abdomen; jejunoileal: distension, many loops.
Omphalocele: midline, covered by sac; gastroschisis: right of cord, no membrane.
Omphalocele has other major malformations (cardiac, genitourinary, neural tube).
Dx: Duodenal atresia: double bubble on abdominal X-ray; exclude malrotation.
Rx: Duodenal: decompression, fluids → surgical repair (duodenoduodenostomy).
Wrap bowel in sterile saline dressings, NG tube; primary closure, else staged silo repair.
High anal atresia: colostomy → PSARP; low → anoplasty.

topics.title: Follow-up of the premature baby Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).

Def: BPD = oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA.
ROP = abnormal retinal vessel growth in preterm babies.
Cause: Prematurity plus oxygen toxicity (RIB), ventilator trauma, infection.
Patho: BPD: arrested alveolar/vascular growth + injury → simplified alveoli, pulmonary hypertension.
ROP: high oxygen → hypoxic retina → VEGF surge → neovascularisation.
Signs: BPD: month of oxygen need, ground-glass opacities on X-ray (scarring).
Follow growth, neurodevelopment (PVL → spastic diplegia), hearing, vision.
Dx: Corrected age for growth/development (~2 years); chronological for vaccines.
ROP screen: <31 weeks or <1501 g; BPD with rising O2 → echo.
Rx: Supplement iron, vitamin D; RSV prevention: nirsevimab or palivizumab.
BPD prevention: maternal glucocorticoids, surfactant, caffeine; oxygen, nutrition.
ROP: laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.

Def: Hodgkin: adolescent lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells; childhood NHL is high grade.
Cause: NHL: Burkitt t(8;14) MYC, lymphoblastic, DLBCL, ALCL.
Hodgkin: nodular sclerosis commonest (70%).
Patho: Hodgkin: reactive inflammatory cells, contiguous spread; cytokines → B symptoms.
Burkitt lysis → TLS: high K, phosphate, urate, low calcium.
Signs: Painless rubbery cervical/supraclavicular nodes; B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10%.
Burkitt: abdominal mass; lymphoblastic: anterior mediastinal mass.
Suspicious node: >2 cm, hard, supraclavicular, persistent.
Dx: Excision biopsy: RS cells CD15, CD30; CXR, PET-CT; staging predicts prognosis.
No steroids before biopsy.
Rx: Hodgkin: response-adapted chemotherapy, cure >90%.
TLS: hyperhydrate, rasburicase (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency).
Mediastinal mass → avoid general anaesthesia and lying flat.

Def: Commonest childhood cancer; ALL ~80%, peak 2-5 years.
Cause: Risk factor: Down syndrome.
Patho: Blasts fill marrow → anaemia, bleeding, infection; infiltration → bone pain, organomegaly; CNS a sanctuary.
Signs: Pallor, bleeding, infection, bone pain, HSM, lymphadenopathy; mediastinal mass in T-ALL.
Dx: Bone marrow examination + flow cytometry, genetics; LP.
Good: age 1-10, WBC <50, hyperdiploidy/ETV6-RUNX1; minimal residual disease strongest.
Rx: Induction, consolidation + intrathecal methotrexate, intensification, maintenance (~2 y); ~90% cure.
Febrile neutropenia → IV antibiotics within 1 hour; co-trimoxazole vs Pneumocystis.
High-risk/relapse: allogeneic SCT; graft versus leukaemia = donor cells attack leukaemic cells.

Def: Low, dysfunctional or high platelets; bleed into skin and mucosa, not joints.
Cause: Destruction (ITP, NAIT, TTP/HUS, DIC, hypersplenism); underproduction (leukaemia, aplasia).
Dysfunction, normal count: Glanzmann, Bernard-Soulier, vWD, aspirin.
Patho: ITP: IgG against GPIIb/IIIa → platelets consumed by splenic macrophages.
TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency → uncleaved vWF → microthrombi; Glanzmann: aggregation defect; Bernard-Soulier: adhesion.
Signs: Petechiae, purpura, epistaxis; feared complication intracranial bleeding.
ITP: well child, purpura 3 weeks after viral illness, no organomegaly.
Dx: ITP: isolated low platelets, large platelets on film, increased megakaryocytes.
Other cell line low, HSM or bone pain → bone marrow; TTP: raised LDH.
Rx: ITP: cutaneous only → observation (75-80% resolve in 6 months); mucosal bleeding → corticosteroids.
Significant bleeding → IVIG; chronic ITP (>12 months): romiplostim/eltrombopag.
TTP: plasma exchange; thrombocytosis is reactive → no treatment, no aspirin.

topics.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation, haemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)

Def: DIC: consumptive coagulation. HUS triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.
TTP: deficiency or inhibition of ADAMTS13 (vWF metalloprotease).
Cause: DIC: sepsis, shock, trauma, malignancy.
Typical HUS follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7).
Atypical HUS: alternative complement pathway dysregulation.
Patho: DIC: tissue factor → microthrombi + consumption + fibrinolysis → clots and bleeds.
Shiga toxin binds Gb3 receptors on glomerular endothelium → microthrombi → RBC fragmentation, AKI.
Signs: DIC: bleeding plus thrombosis.
HUS: anaemia, low platelets, AKI after bloody diarrhoea.
Dx: DIC labs: low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer.
Clotting times are normal in HUS but prolonged in DIC; TTP has raised LDH.
Rx: DIC: treat the cause; platelets, FFP, cryo only if bleeding.
Typical HUS: supportive care, dialysis; avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs.
Atypical HUS → eculizumab; TTP → plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, rituximab.

Def: Inherited haem-synthesis enzyme defects; precursors before the block accumulate.
Cause: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP): autosomal dominant, deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (HMBS).
Porphyria cutanea tarda: UROD deficiency, most common porphyria.
Commonest in children: erythropoietic protoporphyria, ferrochelatase deficiency. Triggers: P-450 inducers, barbiturates contraindicated.
Patho: Early haem precursors (ALA, PBG) are neurotoxic → acute attacks.
Late porphyrins cause photosensitivity.
Signs: AIP mnemonic Wine In PAIN: wine-coloured urine, inducers, psychological disturbance, abdominal pain, neuropathy; no photosensitivity.
Hyponatraemia in an attack is due to SIADH.
PCT: blistering cutaneous photosensitivity and hyperpigmentation.
Dx: Screening test in an acute attack: urinary porphobilinogen; also raised ALA.
Rx: Acute attack: IV haem arginate (haemin) and glucose, which inhibit ALA synthesis.
PCT: low-dose hydroxychloroquine or phlebotomy.

Def: LCH: proliferation of Langerhans cells; HLH: systemic overactivation of macrophages and cytotoxic T cells.
Cause: LCH: BRAF V600E, peak 1-3 years; Hand-Schüller-Christian often in children over 3.
HLH: primary genetic or secondary to EBV, systemic JIA.
Patho: LCH cells are positive for CD1a and CD207 (langerin); infiltrate bone, skin, pituitary, organs.
HLH: failed perforin cytotoxicity → cytokine storm.
Signs: LCH: lytic (punched-out) skull lesion, painful lytic long-bone lesion with normocalcaemia, skin rash.
Pituitary involvement causes central diabetes insipidus.
HLH: fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly.
Dx: LCH: biopsy + staging; risk organs are liver, spleen and bone marrow.
HLH shows very high ferritin, high triglycerides, low fibrinogen.
Rx: Multisystem LCH needs systemic chemotherapy; single bone lesion may need only curettage or observation.
HLH: immunosuppression (steroids ± chemotherapy); primary (familial) HLH needs HSCT.

topics.title: Central nervous system tumours in children

Def: CNS tumours are the commonest solid tumours of childhood.
In children, primary CNS tumours are usually infratentorial; about half are posterior fossa.
Cause: Pilocytic astrocytoma: commonest primary CNS tumour; good prognosis.
Medulloblastoma (primitive neuroectodermal, cerebellar granule cells); ependymoma in the 4th ventricle.
Turcot syndrome: FAP + malignant CNS tumours. Pineal tumours → Parinaud syndrome.
Patho: Posterior fossa mass → obstructive hydrocephalus → raised ICP.
Medulloblastoma grows rapidly, spreads via CSF (drop metastasis); pilocytic = cyst + mural nodule.
Signs: Raised ICP headache worst on waking (nocturnal CO₂ retention → vasodilatation); vomiting.
Ependymoma: relief in the knee-chest position. Parinaud: upward gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus.
Dx: Urgent MRI of brain and spine, and no lumbar puncture with raised ICP.
Ependymoma: perivascular pseudorosettes; medulloblastoma: MYC amplification.
Rx: Maximal safe resection; dexamethasone, CSF diversion for hydrocephalus.
Cranial radiotherapy is avoided under about 3 years; chemotherapy; lifelong late-effect follow-up.

Def: Neuroblastoma: arises from sympathetic neural crest cells, most often the adrenal medulla.
Wilms tumour: malignant kidney tumour of metanephric mesenchyme (blastema).
Cause: Neuroblastoma: N-myc (MYCN) amplification is the strongest adverse marker.
Wilms: 3-4 years; WAGR = Wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, developmental delay.
Patho: Neuroblastoma: small blue round cells, Homer-Wright rosettes; markers bombesin and NSE.
Wilms spreads most often to the lungs.
Signs: Neuroblastoma: abdominal mass, periorbital ecchymoses (orbital bone metastases), opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.
Wilms: smooth flank mass that does not cross the midline in a well child aged 3-4 years.
Dx: Any abdominal mass → same-day review + ultrasound (Wilms: abdominal ultrasound).
Neuroblastoma: urinary VMA and HVA raised; MIBG, marrow, biopsy.
Rx: Neuroblastoma high-risk: chemo, surgery, stem cell rescue, radiotherapy, anti-GD2.
Wilms: Europe (SIOP) gives chemotherapy before surgery; the US (COG) usually operates first.

topics.title: Malignant bone and soft tissue tumours

Def: Osteosarcoma: malignant proliferation of osteoblasts; peak 10-20 years.
Ewing sarcoma: neuroectoderm-derived; rhabdomyosarcoma: commonest soft tissue sarcoma of childhood.
Cause: Ewing carries t(11;22) (EWSR1-FLI1); boys.
Osteosarcoma: hereditary retinoblastoma, Li-Fraumeni, prior radiation.
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides): girls.
Patho: Osteosarcoma arises in the metaphysis of long bones, often knee; cells make osteoid.
Ewing: small round blue cells in the diaphysis (femur).
Commonest metastasis site: lungs.
Signs: Osteosarcoma: painful enlarging mass, pathological fracture, bone pain with swelling.
Ewing may mimic osteomyelitis. Sarcoma botryoides: grape-like vaginal mass with bleeding.
Soft tissue lump >2 cm, deep, enlarging or painful → urgent ultrasound.
Dx: Osteosarcoma X-ray: sunburst and Codman triangle; Ewing: onion-skin periosteal reaction.
Rhabdomyoblasts stain for desmin and myogenin; soft tissue sarcoma → core needle biopsy.
Rx: Osteosarcoma: en bloc resection and chemotherapy; radio-resistant.
Ewing is radiosensitive: chemo + surgery and/or radiotherapy.
Soft tissue sarcoma: wide excision, chemotherapy, radiation.

topics.title: Early and late onset adverse effects of chemotherapy

Def: Chemotherapeutic drugs are effective against rapidly dividing cells → early and late toxicities.
Cause: High-turnover tissues (marrow, mucosa, hair) plus drug-specific organ toxicity.
Etoposide (topoisomerase II inhibitor) is linked to secondary AML.
Patho: Marrow nadir 7-14 d → neutropenia → infection risk.
Tumour lysis syndrome: high potassium, high phosphate, high urate, low calcium.
Signs: Anthracyclines → dilated cardiomyopathy; cisplatin → high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, renal magnesium wasting.
Cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide → haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein); vincristine → peripheral neuropathy, constipation, paralytic ileus.
Bleomycin → lung fibrosis, mucositis; vinblastine → myelosuppression.
Dx: Febrile neutropenia = emergency → cultures.
Late effects: cardiac, gonadal, endocrine, neurocognitive and second cancers.
Rx: Febrile neutropenia: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.
Protect with dexrazoxane (anthracyclines) and mesna (cyclophosphamide); rasburicase contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Vincristine is fatal if given intrathecally; lifelong follow-up.
· Thesis line

topics.title: Diabetes mellitus. Management of diabetic ketoacidosis

Def: Type 1 DM: autoimmune beta-cell destruction → absolute insulin deficiency; peaks 4-6 y, puberty.
Four symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss despite good appetite, fatigue.
Cause: Autoimmune: antibodies to GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin.
Commonest associated autoimmune diseases: coeliac disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Patho: No insulin → hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → dehydration.
Ketone production → acidosis → Kussmaul breathing; total body K⁺ depleted.
Signs: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss despite good appetite, fatigue; secondary enuresis.
DKA: vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, drowsiness.
Dx: Typical symptoms + high glucose (18.2 mmol/L) → paediatric diabetes centre immediately.
DKA: glucose >11 mmol/L, venous pH, plus ketones.
Rx: DKA: fluids, then insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h with no bolus; potassium, dextrose.
Leading cause of death: cerebral oedema (headache, bradycardia) → mannitol or 3% saline.
Most modern: insulin pump with an integrated glucose sensor.

Def: Metabolic syndrome: central obesity + ≥ 2 of high TG, low HDL, HTN, high fasting glucose.
T2DM: obese pubertal teen; islet autoantibodies negative, high C-peptide.
Cause: Central obesity, puberty, family history of T2DM, high-risk ethnic group.
MODY: autosomal dominant, 3 generations, not obese.
Patho: Visceral fat → insulin resistance → hyperinsulinaemia + free fatty acids → the cluster.
Insulin resistance → acanthosis nigricans, fatty liver, PCOS.
Signs: Thick, dark, velvety skin in neck and axillae: acanthosis nigricans.
Often asymptomatic on screening; polyuria, polydipsia, occasionally DKA; raised ALT, sleep apnoea, SCFE.
Dx: Type 1 vs type 2: islet autoantibodies and C-peptide in every new case.
GCK-MODY: mild stable fasting hyperglycaemia. Diabetes <6 months → genetic testing.
Rx: First-line drug without ketosis: metformin plus lifestyle; insulin if ketosis or HbA1c ≥ 8.5%.
HNF1A-MODY very sensitive to sulfonylureas; GCK-MODY needs no treatment.
Screen complications from diagnosis.

Def: Central DI = deficient vasopressin (ADH); nephrogenic DI = renal resistance to it.
Dilute polyuria.
Cause: Central: craniopharyngioma, germinoma, LCH, trauma, neurosurgery, meningitis.
Nephrogenic: X-linked AVPR2, lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia.
Patho: No ADH or V2 resistance → no aquaporin-2 in collecting duct → dilute urine.
Free water loss → ↑ plasma osm → thirst; infants → hypernatraemic dehydration.
Signs: Polyuria >2 L/m²/day, nocturia, secondary enuresis.
Intense thirst, prefers cold water; infant FTT, vomiting, fever.
Dx: DI confirmed by high plasma osmolality with urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg.
After water deprivation, desmopressin concentrates urine by >50% in central DI, not nephrogenic.
Central DI needs MRI: craniopharyngioma, germinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Rx: Central → desmopressin; main risk is hyponatraemia.
Nephrogenic → low-solute diet and thiazide diuretics; stop lithium.
Correct hypernatraemia ≤ 0.5 mmol/L per hour.

Def: Hypo- or hyperfunction of anterior (GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin) or posterior (vasopressin) pituitary.
Cause: Congenital: midline defects - septo-optic dysplasia, cleft palate, single central incisor.
Acquired: craniopharyngioma, cranial irradiation, trauma, histiocytosis, infection.
Patho: GH deficiency → low growth velocity, delayed bone age, normal proportions.
Craniopharyngioma compresses the optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia; DI.
Signs: Newborn hypopituitarism: hypoglycaemia, micropenis, prolonged jaundice.
Prolactinoma: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea. Weight gain with falling height velocity suggests Cushing syndrome.
Posterior: DI, or SIADH.
Dx: Low IGF-1 → failure of two GH stimulation tests → pituitary MRI.
Craniopharyngioma: suprasellar, cystic and calcified.
Rx: GHD → recombinant GH until final height.
Always replace cortisol before thyroxine.
Prolactinoma: cabergoline; craniopharyngioma → surgery ± radiotherapy; SIADH → fluid restriction.

Def: CAH: AR defect of cortisol synthesis; ~95% 21-hydroxylase deficiency, commonest adrenocortical enzyme defect.
Cause: Autosomal recessive CYP21A2 mutation.
Rare: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (virilisation and hypertension), 17α-hydroxylase.
Patho: Low cortisol → no feedback → ACTH up → adrenal hyperplasia.
Salt-wasting: insufficient glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid, excessive androgen.
Signs: Girls: virilised genitalia at birth.
Boys: salt-wasting crisis at 1-3 weeks - hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, low glucose, shock.
Simple virilising: precocious pseudopuberty.
Dx: Diagnostic marker: raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone (newborn screening); high ACTH and renin.
Karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, CYP21A2 genetics.
Rx: Crisis: IV hydrocortisone, 0.9% saline 10-20 mL/kg, IV dextrose.
Long-term: hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and salt in infancy.
Stress dosing in illness; emergency card.

Def: Congenital or acquired hypothyroidism; hyperthyroidism mostly Graves (Basedow's disease, TRAb-driven).
Cause: Commonest congenital cause: thyroid dysgenesis (~85%), most often an ectopic gland.
Maternal iodine deficiency → temporary primary hypothyroidism in the newborn.
Acquired: Hashimoto thyroiditis, commonest in children.
Patho: No hormone → slowed metabolism, growth and brain development → delayed bone age.
TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies → gland overdrive → thyrotoxicosis.
Signs: Neonate: prolonged jaundice, constipation, hypotonia, macroglossia, umbilical hernia.
Hashimoto: painless goitre, growth failure.
Basedow's: weight loss, tachycardia, Graefe sign.
Dx: Heel-prick TSH day 3-5.
Hashimoto: high TSH, low free T4, anti-TPO. Graves: suppressed TSH, high T4/T3, TRAb.
Rx: Congenital: levothyroxine 10-15 µg/kg/day within the first 2 weeks.
Graves: methimazole + propranolol; propylthiouracil is avoided because of severe hepatotoxicity.
Sore throat/fever → urgent blood count.

topics.title: Disorders of calcium and phosphorus homeostasis. Rickets.

Def: Rickets = failed growth-plate mineralisation; mostly vitamin D deficiency in unsupplemented breastfed infants.
Cause: Commonest: vitamin D deficiency - unsupplemented breastfeeding, dark skin, little sunlight.
Phosphopenic: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (PHEX, high FGF23), Fanconi syndrome.
Patho: Low vitamin D → less Ca/P absorption → PTH rises → phosphate wasting.
Low Ca × P → growth plate cannot mineralise → deformity.
Signs: Soft, ping-pong-ball skull bones = craniotabes; rachitic rosary, Harrison sulcus, wide wrists, bowed legs.
Infants <6 mo: hypocalcaemic seizures, tetany, laryngospasm.
Dx: Nutritional rickets bloods: phosphate low, ALP very high, PTH high.
XLH: low phosphate with normal calcium and normal PTH.
X-ray: cupping, fraying and splaying of the metaphyses.
Rx: Prevent: all infants receive 400 IU of vitamin D daily.
Nutritional: high-dose vitamin D ≥ 12 weeks + calcium; XLH: phosphate + calcitriol or burosumab.
Hypocalcaemia that won't correct with IV calcium - check magnesium.

Def: Multisystem autoimmune disease: immune complexes against nuclear antigens.
cSLE: adolescent girls, more severe than adult disease.
Cause: Female predominance after puberty; more common in non-white populations.
Anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid).
Patho: Immune complexes deposit → organ damage; in active SLE complement C3 and C4 fall.
Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies cause congenital heart block.
Signs: Fever, malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, painless oral ulcers.
Non-erosive arthritis, serositis, nephritis 50-80%, seizures/psychosis.
Coombs-positive haemolysis, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia.
Dx: Entry criterion: ANA at a titre of at least 1:80.
Anti-dsDNA tracks activity and nephritis; anti-Sm most specific.
High CRP in a febrile lupus patient suggests infection, not flare.
Rx: Every SLE patient takes hydroxychloroquine + sun protection.
Moderate → azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate.
Severe → IV methylprednisolone → mycophenolate or IV cyclophosphamide; rituximab if refractory.

Def: JDM: autoimmune small-vessel vasculopathy of skin and muscle; commonest childhood myopathy.
Commonest scleroderma in children: localised (linear); systemic sclerosis rare.
Cause: JDM peaks 5-10 y, girls more often.
Patho: Complement deposition → capillary loss in muscle and skin → weakness, rash, ulcers.
Rarely linked to malignancy (unlike adults) → no routine cancer screening.
Signs: Weakness of the proximal muscles of the limbs and neck flexors; Gowers sign.
Purple eyelids = heliotrope rash; red scaly papules over knuckles = Gottron papules.
Calcinosis much commoner than in adult dermatomyositis.
Dx: CK, LDH, AST/ALT, aldolase + MRI (T2/STIR) muscle oedema.
Biopsy: perifascicular atrophy. SSc antibodies: anti-Scl-70, anticentromere.
Rx: First-line JDM: steroids plus methotrexate; IVIG if severe.
Localised scleroderma: methotrexate ± initial steroids; physiotherapy.
SSc: CCB for Raynaud, ACE inhibitor for renal crisis.

Def: Commonest vasculitis of childhood: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), small vessel, 3-10 years.
Cause: Follows upper respiratory infection (often streptococcal); autumn and winter.
Takayasu is large-vessel, Kawasaki medium-vessel; granulomatosis with polyangiitis: c-ANCA (PR3).
Patho: IgA small-vessel vasculitis → palpable purpura with a normal platelet count.
Gut → colic, bleeding, ileo-ileal intussusception; kidney → haematuria, proteinuria.
Signs: Palpable purpura on buttocks and legs (always).
Arthritis of ankles/knees (~75%); colicky abdominal pain (~50-75%).
Nephritis (~20-50%) usually within 4-6 weeks.
Dx: Clinical: purpura (mandatory) + abdominal pain, IgA histology, arthritis or renal involvement.
FBC/clotting normal; urine protein-creatinine ratio, BP; US if severe pain.
Rx: Supportive: rest, paracetamol (acetaminophen), fluids; NSAIDs only if kidneys normal.
Steroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis.
Monitor urine and blood pressure for 6-12 months.

topics.title: Urinary tract infections, localisation, course, treatment, complications, VUR

Def: UTI: cystitis (bladder mucosa) vs pyelonephritis (renal parenchyma).
Cause: Most frequent pathogen: E. coli (P fimbriae); Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus.
Risks: VUR, posterior urethral valves, constipation, dysfunctional voiding.
Patho: Bowel flora ascends; primary VUR is caused by a short intramural ureteric tunnel.
Pyelonephritis → fever, high CRP → renal scarring → HTN, CKD.
Signs: Infants: non-specific - fever, vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice, sepsis.
Older: dysuria, frequency (cystitis) vs fever, loin pain (pyelonephritis).
Dx: Clean/catheter sample: dipstick nitrite + leucocyte esterase, culture.
Pyelonephritis sediment: leucocytes, white blood cell casts and bacteria.
VUR: MCU, sonocystography, dynamic kidney scintigraphy; DMSA scan 4-6 months later shows scarring.
Rx: Infants under 3 months: admit, IV antibiotics (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone).
Pyelonephritis: oral cefalexin or co-amoxiclav 7-10 days; cystitis 3 days.
VUR: fix bowel/bladder, prophylaxis; surgery for breakthrough infections.

Def: Urinary tract stones in children; mostly metabolic.
Cause: Commonest metabolic abnormality: hypercalciuria; also hypocitraturia, hyperoxaluria, cystinuria, distal RTA.
Infection (Proteus), anatomical stasis, drugs (furosemide in preterms, topiramate).
Patho: Excess solute + little water + low citrate (main inhibitor) → supersaturation → crystals.
Struvite forms in alkaline urine via urease-producing organisms such as Proteus.
Signs: Adolescents: renal colic flank → groin, nausea, haematuria.
Young children: atypical - vague pain, irritability, UTI, painless haematuria.
Hexagonal crystals in urine indicate cystinuria.
Dx: First-line imaging: ultrasound; KUB for calcium stones; low-dose CT only if unclear.
Metabolic work-up in every child: blood + urine calcium, oxalate, citrate, cystine; stone analysis.
Rx: NSAIDs + paracetamol, hydration; obstructed infected kidney → urgent drainage.
<5 mm usually pass (tamsulosin); else ESWL, ureteroscopy, PCNL for staghorn.
Prevent: fluids, low salt, thiazide (reduces urinary calcium), potassium citrate, tiopronin for cystine.

Def: Glomerulonephritis: glomerular inflammation → haematuria ± proteinuria; nephritic syndrome.
Cause: Most frequent type: IgA nephropathy; PSGN after group A strep.
Others: lupus, MPGN, HSP nephritis, ANCA, anti-GBM.
Haematuria with sensorineural deafness suggests Alport syndrome.
Patho: Immune complexes break GBM → red cells + casts, proteinuria.
↓ GFR + ongoing Na⁺ reabsorption → oedema, hypertension, oliguria.
Signs: Cola urine, periorbital oedema, hypertension, oliguria.
IgA: macroscopic haematuria 1-2 days after URTI. PSGN: 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis, 3-6 weeks after impetigo.
Dx: Urine: red blood cells with red blood cell casts, most commonly with proteinuria.
IgA: normal C3. PSGN: C3 low, normalises by 6-8 weeks; ASO/anti-DNase B.
Rx: PSGN: supportive - fluid/salt restriction, furosemide, antihypertensives, penicillin.
IgA: ACE inhibitor; steroids for heavier disease.
RPGN: pulse methylprednisolone + immunosuppression; plasma exchange if anti-GBM.

Def: Heavy proteinuria (UPCR ≥ 200 mg/mmol), albumin <30 g/L, oedema, + hyperlipidaemia.
Cause: Commonest cause in young children: minimal change disease, age 2-6, boys, ~80-90%.
Atypical if <1 or >12 y, HTN, macroscopic haematuria, low C3, renal impairment.
Patho: Circulating factor → podocyte effacement → selective albumin leak → low oncotic pressure → oedema.
Thrombosis: urinary loss of antithrombin III; lost IgG → infection.
Signs: Periorbital oedema in the morning → legs, scrotum, ascites, effusions.
Peritonitis classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae; also renal vein thrombosis, hypovolaemia/AKI.
Dx: Urine protein-creatinine ratio, serum albumin, lipids.
No remission after 4 weeks of daily prednisolone = steroid-resistant; needs biopsy and genetic testing.
Rx: First episode: oral prednisolone daily for 4 weeks, then alternate days for 4 weeks.
Albumin 20% for symptomatic hypovolaemia; pneumococcal vaccine; no added salt.
Relapsing/dependent → CNI, mycophenolate, rituximab; resistant → CNI + ACE inhibitor.

topics.title: Acute and chronic kidney failure. Kidney transplantation.

Def: KDIGO AKI: creatinine rise ≥ 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) in 48 h or ≥ 1.5× in 7 days.
CKD: abnormal structure/function >3 months; G5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m².
Cause: Pre-renal commonest; post-renal: PUV.
Intrinsic AKI after bloody diarrhoea: HUS; commonest CKD cause: CAKUT.
Patho: Low perfusion → Na and water kept → FENa <1%; BUN rises relatively more.
No K⁺ excretion → hyperkalaemia → arrhythmia.
CKD: ↓ erythropoietin → anaemia; PTH ↑, Ca²⁺ ↓, phosphorus ↑.
Signs: Oliguria, fluid overload, hypertension, uraemia.
CKD: anaemia, bone disease, HTN, growth failure.
HUS triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.
Dx: Creatinine, urine sodium, ultrasound; hyperkalaemia ECG: peaked T, wide QRS.
Rx: Treat cause, stop nephrotoxins, balance fluids (insensible 300-400 mL/m²/day + UO).
Hyperkalaemia: IV calcium gluconate → salbutamol/insulin-glucose → resin → dialyse.
CKD: ESA, binders; pre-emptive living-donor transplantation; atypical HUS: eculizumab.

topics.title: Developmental abnormalities of the kidneys and the urinary tract

Def: CAKUT: congenital kidney/urinary tract anomalies - commonest cause of childhood CKD.
Cause: Failed ureteric bud-mesenchyme induction → agenesis, dysplasia; abnormal ascent → horseshoe kidney.
Duplex kidney: upper-pole ureter obstructs, lower refluxes; PUJ, PUV obstruct.
Patho: Bilateral agenesis → oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence).
PUV → back-pressure → renal dysplasia, CKD; short intravesical ureter → VUR.
VUR → pyelonephritis → focal scars → hypertension, CKD.
Signs: Antenatal hydronephrosis: commonest cause (normal ureter) PUJ obstruction.
PUV (boys): commonest lower tract obstruction; poor stream, palpable bladder, UTI.
VUR: recurrent pyelonephritis; siblings ~30%. Horseshoe kidney: under inferior mesenteric artery.
Dx: US after first days (early scans underestimate dilatation).
VUR diagnosed and graded (I-V) with MCUG; MAG3 drainage; scars on DMSA.
Rx: PUJ → pyeloplasty if function falls.
PUV → urgent bladder catheter → endoscopic valve ablation.
VUR: treat UTIs, prophylaxis if high grade; reimplantation for breakthrough infection.

Def: Inherited tubular transporter defects, mapped to nephron segments.
Cause: Proximal: Fanconi (commonest cause in children: cystinosis); loop: Bartter; DCT: Gitelman.
Collecting duct: distal RTA, type 4 RTA, nephrogenic DI (X-linked AVPR2).
Patho: Bartter/Gitelman: salt wasting → renin, aldosterone up → hypokalaemic alkalosis.
Distal RTA: no H+ secretion → normal-gap acidosis; urine pH stays >5.5; hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia → nephrocalcinosis.
Signs: Fanconi: glycosuria with normal blood glucose (proximal tubulopathy), phosphaturia → rickets, failure to thrive.
Bartter mimics furosemide and causes hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, polyhydramnios.
Gitelman mimics thiazides and causes hypomagnesaemia, hypocalciuria, cramps, tetany.
Dx: Blood gas, K, Mg, urine pH and calcium; cystinosis → corneal crystals.
Nephrogenic DI: dilute urine, hypernatraemia, no response to desmopressin.
Rx: Cystinosis: cysteamine + replace water, bicarbonate, phosphate, K.
Bartter: indometacin + K; Gitelman: Mg + K.
Distal RTA: alkali (citrate); nephrogenic DI: free water, thiazide.

Def: Numerical or structural chromosome errors: trisomies, microdeletions, sex chromosome aneuploidies.
Cause: Down syndrome: ~95% non-disjunction (maternal age), ~4% translocation (karyotype the parents), ~1% mosaic.
Trisomy 18/13; 22q11 deletion; Williams 7q11.23; Turner 45,X; Klinefelter 47,XXY.
Patho: Down: extra copies of APP gene → early Alzheimer; endocardial cushion defect → AVSD.
22q11 deletion: thymic hypoplasia → infections; parathyroid hypoplasia → hypocalcaemia.
Turner short stature: SHOX haploinsufficiency.
Signs: Down: hypotonia, duodenal atresia (trisomy 21), Hirschsprung, leukaemia, hypothyroid.
Edwards: clenched fists, overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet; Patau: holoprosencephaly, cleft lip, polydactyly.
22q11: conotruncal heart defects; Turner: webbed neck, coarctation; Klinefelter: tall, small firm testes, infertility.
Dx: Prenatal: combined first-trimester test, NIPT → CVS/amniocentesis with QF-PCR/karyotype.
Translocation Down → karyotype parents; microdeletions → microarray, FISH.
Rx: Down: screen heart, thyroid, hearing, eyes, coeliac; multidisciplinary care.
Turner: growth hormone + oestrogen; check for Y material (gonadoblastoma).
Klinefelter: testosterone at puberty.

topics.title: Mendelian inherited diseases (autosomal dominant and recessive), common disorders

Def: Single-gene disease: AD needs one mutant allele; AR needs both.
Cause: AD: NF1, Marfan (fibrillin-1), achondroplasia (FGFR3 gain-of-function), TSC, ADPKD, FH.
AR: CF, PKU, SMA (SMN1 deletion), sickle, CAH, galactosaemia, Wilson.
Patho: AD: haploinsufficiency, dominant negative, gain of function; de novo mutations common, linked to advanced paternal age.
AR: most enzyme deficiencies are AR because 50% activity is sufficient, so carriers are healthy.
Signs: AD pedigree: vertical, each child has 50% risk, male-to-male transmission.
AR pedigree: horizontal, two carrier parents → 25% risk per pregnancy; consanguinity.
Healthy sibling of an AR child: 2/3 carrier; meconium ileus → cystic fibrosis.
Dx: Mutation analysis, gene panels, exome/genome sequencing; carrier screening.
Prenatal (CVS, amniocentesis); newborn screening for PKU, CAH, galactosaemia, CF, SMA.
Rx: Non-directive genetic counselling with risk calculation.
Cascade testing of relatives; disease-specific therapy (e.g.
nusinersen for SMA).

Def: XLR: affected boys, carrier mothers, no male-to-male transmission.
XLD: both sexes; affected father → all daughters affected.
Cause: A carrier mother has a 50% risk of each son being affected.
Haemophilia father: all daughters obligate carriers; ~1/3 of Duchenne new mutations.
Patho: Males hemizygous; lyonisation protects most carriers.
Duchenne: out-of-frame dystrophin deletion; Becker: in-frame one.
Fragile X: CGG repeat in FMR1; XLA: BTK.
Signs: DMD age 2-5: Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, falls.
Haemophilia: haemarthrosis; fragile X: ID, long face; XLA: infections from ~6 months.
WAS: eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, infections; XLD: hypophosphataemic rickets, Rett syndrome.
Dx: First test in suspected Duchenne: serum creatine kinase (>10 000 U/L) → genetic testing.
Haemophilia: isolated long APTT, normal PT and platelets.
Rx: DMD: corticosteroids (prednisolone [prednisone] or deflazacort), physio, cardiac/respiratory surveillance.
Avoid suxamethonium; haemophilia: factor prophylaxis, emicizumab, no IM/NSAIDs.
Live vaccines must be avoided in XLA.

Def: Disease appears when combined genetic and environmental liability crosses a threshold.
Cause: Boys: pyloric stenosis (about 4-5 times commoner in boys), cleft lip, Hirschsprung, club foot.
Girls: DDH, isolated cleft palate, NTDs; also CHD, diabetes, asthma.
Patho: Relatives share genes → curve shifts toward threshold → empiric recurrence.
Carter effect: when the less commonly affected sex is affected, relatives have a higher recurrence risk.
Signs: First-degree recurrence of an isolated malformation is 2-5%; falls sharply in second-degree relatives.
Risk ↑ with severity, ≥ 2 affected relatives, affected rarer sex.
Dx: Other anomalies/dysmorphism/delay → look for syndrome (22q11, trisomy 13) first.
NTD screening: raised maternal serum AFP + anomaly ultrasound.
Rx: Counsel with empiric risks; NTD recurrence ~3-5% without folate.
Folic acid 400 µg (all) or 5 mg daily (high-risk woman) preconception to 12 weeks.
US: 4 mg after previous NTD pregnancy.

topics.title: Congenital metabolic disorders of amino acid metabolism

Def: Mostly autosomal recessive enzyme defects of amino acid metabolism.
Cause: Classic PKU: deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase; MSUD: branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.
Tyrosinaemia 1: fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase; homocystinuria: cystathionine β -synthase.
Patho: Placenta clears metabolites → well at birth → sick after protein feeds.
PKU: low tyrosine (precursor of melanin) → fair hair; leucine → cerebral oedema.
Signs: Sepsis-like: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, coma.
Untreated PKU: musty odour; sweet-smelling urine + neonatal encephalopathy: maple syrup urine disease.
Tyrosinaemia 1: liver failure + Fanconi; homocystinuria: marfanoid, lens dislocates downwards (Marfan: upwards).
Dx: PKU: newborn heel-prick phenylalanine.
Crisis: glucose, gas, lactate, ammonia, amino acids, urine organic acids.
Rx: Acute metabolic crisis: stop protein and give high-energy IV glucose (10%).
Ammonia scavengers/haemofiltration, treat sepsis; PKU: lifelong low-Phe diet ± sapropterin.
Tyrosinaemia → nitisinone; homocystinuria → pyridoxine (B6); MSUD → BCAA-restricted diet.

topics.title: Congenital metabolic disorders of glucose and glycogen metabolism

Def: Inherited defects of glycogen, galactose or fructose metabolism.
Cause: Von Gierke (GSD I) is deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (AR).
Pompe (GSD II), McArdle (GSD V), galactosaemia (GALT), fructose intolerance (aldolase B); MCAD: AR.
Patho: G6Pase block → raised lactate, uric acid and triglycerides.
MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting.
Signs: Low blood sugar in an infant with normal temperature and hepatomegaly: von Gierke disease.
Pompe: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and hypotonia; McArdle: exercise cramps, myoglobinuria, second wind.
Neonatal jaundice, cataract, E. coli sepsis after milk: galactosaemia; hereditary fructose intolerance at weaning.
Dx: GSD I: fasting hypoglycaemia 2-4 h post-feed, lactic acidosis, high urate.
Galactosaemia: red-cell GALT, urine reducing substances; McArdle: raised CK.
Rx: GSD I: never fast - frequent/overnight feeds, uncooked cornstarch, allopurinol.
Pompe: enzyme replacement; galactosaemia: stop lactose now, soy formula.
MCAD: avoid fasting; fructose intolerance: exclude fructose, sucrose, sorbitol.

Def: Lysosomal enzyme deficiency → substrate stored in the cells that turn over most.
Cause: Mostly recessive; the two X-linked ones: Fabry and Hunter.
Gaucher is deficiency of β -glucocerebrosidase; Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs (hex A), Hurler ( α -L-iduronidase), Pompe.
Patho: Macrophage → hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias; neuron → regression, cherry-red spot.
Connective tissue (GAGs) → coarse face, dysostosis multiplex, valves, corneal clouding.
Signs: Normal at birth, then loss of skills = key alarm.
Cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly: Tay-Sachs; with hepatosplenomegaly: Niemann-Pick.
Gaucher: massive splenomegaly, bone crises; Hurler: corneal clouding (Hunter: none); Fabry: burning hands/feet.
Dx: Enzyme activity in leucocytes or dried blood spots.
Urinary GAGs/oligosaccharides, genetic testing; newborn screening for Pompe, MPS I.
Rx: ERT does not treat CNS disease: it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
Gaucher, Fabry, Hunter: ERT; substrate reduction.
HSCT before ~2 y in Hurler preserves cognition; multidisciplinary supportive care.

Def: Upper airway inflammation: rhinitis, adenoid hypertrophy, tonsillitis.
Cause: Rhinitis: viral or allergic (IgE).
Tonsillitis: mostly viral; group A strep commonest bacterial, 5-15 years.
Patho: Adenoid hypertrophy peaks at 3-7 years: blocked nose, Eustachian tubes → snoring, OSA, otitis media.
GAS → rheumatic fever; PSGN follows pharyngitis by 1-2 weeks.
Signs: Allergic: sneezing, itch; unilateral foul discharge in a toddler = foreign body.
GAS: fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough.
Trismus, hot-potato voice and deviated uvula: peritonsillar abscess (quinsy).
Dx: GAS: rapid antigen test; negative backed by throat culture (low sensitivity).
Adenoids: nasendoscopy or lateral neck X-ray; sleep study if OSA uncertain.
Rx: Allergic rhinitis: most effective is an intranasal steroid; viral: no antibiotics.
GAS: penicillin V for 10 days (prevents rheumatic fever, not PSGN); avoid amoxicillin if EBV possible.
Adenectomy: recurrent URTIs, otitis media, blocked nasal breathing, OSA; tonsillectomy: 7/1 y, 5/y×2, 3/y×3.

topics.title: Acute upper respiratory tract infections, acute sinusitis, bronchitis

Def: Upper airway infections: pharyngitis, sinusitis, croup, epiglottitis, bronchitis - mostly viral.
Cause: Viral: adenovirus, rhinovirus, EBV; croup = parainfluenza.
Bacterial: GAS; sinusitis and otitis media: S. pneumoniae.
Patho: Cold swells ostiomeatal complex → sinus can't drain → bacterial colonisation.
Croup: subglottic oedema in cricoid ring → small radius → high resistance.
Signs: Strep: fever, exudate, tender nodes, no cough.
Croup: barking cough, stridor; epiglottitis: drooling and tripod posture; bronchiolitis: wheeze, not stridor.
Pertussis in young infants: apnoea and cyanosis, often no whoop.
Dx: Bacterial sinusitis: over 10 days, double worsening, or severe onset; CT only for complications.
Strep: rapid antigen test or culture. Epiglottitis: do not examine the throat.
Rx: Antibiotics only: Streptococcus angina, acute otitis media, acute bacterial sinusitis; not colds or bronchiolitis.
Penicillin V for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever; croup: single oral dexamethasone.
Epiglottitis: secure the airway; oseltamivir within 48 hours.

Def: AOM: middle-ear infection; OME: effusion without infection; otitis externa: canal infection.
Cause: Commonest bacterial cause of AOM: S. pneumoniae, NTHi, Moraxella; day-care, smoking, Down.
Otitis externa: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Patho: Children get AOM because their Eustachian tube is short, horizontal and floppy.
Cold → tube blocks → effusion → bulging drum; perforation → otorrhoea.
OME: fluid dampens drum → conductive hearing loss.
Signs: AOM: otalgia, ear-pulling, fever, bulging drum.
OME: dull retracted drum, type B tympanogram.
Typical sign of otitis externa: pain and/or sensitivity of the tragus.
Dx: Otoscopy; tympanometry for OME.
Protruding ear with postauricular swelling after AOM suggests mastoiditis → IV antibiotics, CT.
Rx: AOM: analgesia first; amoxicillin if under 2 years with bilateral disease or otorrhoea.
OME: wait 3 months; grommets in chronic serous otitis media or Eustachian tube dysfunction.
Externa: aural toilet, topical antibiotic ± steroid drops.

topics.title: Pneumonia and complications in infants and children

Def: Lung infection with alveolar exudate; complications are effusion, empyema, abscess.
Cause: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; preschool: viruses commonest overall.
Typical pneumonia: most commonly S. pneumoniae; school age: Mycoplasma; pneumatoceles after influenza → S. aureus.
Patho: Alveolar exudate → low compliance + shunt → tachypnoea, indrawing, grunting, hypoxaemia.
Parapneumonic effusion stages: exudative, fibrinopurulent, organising.
Signs: WHO tachypnoea threshold for age 1-5 years: 40/min ( ≥ 60 <2 mo, ≥ 50 2-12 mo).
Crackles, bronchial breathing, dullness; abdominal pain from diaphragmatic pleura.
Fever persisting after 48 hours of antibiotics suggests empyema or abscess.
Dx: Clinical; CXR not routine if managed at home.
Admit if SpO₂ <92%, grunting, apnoea, poor feeding; US shows effusion septations.
Rx: First-line oral antibiotic for childhood CAP: amoxicillin; add macrolide if Mycoplasma.
Severe: IV ampicillin/penicillin G or ceftriaxone (US); co-amoxiclav/cefuroxime (UK).
Empyema: drain; thick pus dissolved by fibrinolysis (urokinase/streptokinase) → VATS if fails.

Def: Congenital anomalies of diaphragm, lung parenchyma and chest wall.
Cause: CDH is usually a left posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect: pleuroperitoneal canal fails to close.
CPAM, sequestration, lobar emphysema; two most frequent chest deformities: pectus excavatum and pectus carinatum.
Patho: CDH: gut in chest → pulmonary hypoplasia + pulmonary hypertension drive mortality.
Lobar emphysema most often affects the left upper lobe: deficient cartilage → ball-valve.
Signs: CDH: cyanosis, scaphoid abdomen, heart sounds displaced to the right.
CPAM/sequestration: recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe, distress.
Dx: Often antenatal ultrasound; CPAM = cysts that communicate with the airway.
Sequestration has a systemic arterial supply, usually from the aorta (Doppler/CT angiography).
Pectus: Haller index on CT/MRI, echocardiography, spirometry.
Rx: In suspected CDH avoid bag-and-mask ventilation; intubate, NG tube on suction; NO/ECMO, repair when stable.
CPAM/sequestration/lobar emphysema: resection if symptomatic.
Pectus excavatum: Nuss procedure; carinatum: compressive brace.

Def: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect; commonest mutation F508del causes protein misfolding.
Cause: Carrier ~1 in 25 Europeans; class II F508del, class III gating (G551D).
Patho: No Cl⁻ secretion + unopposed ENaC → dehydrated mucus → infection → bronchiectasis.
Blocked pancreatic ducts → exocrine insufficiency; sweat duct cannot reabsorb chloride → salty sweat.
Signs: Meconium ileus (X-ray: soap-bubble; contrast enema: microcolon), steatorrhoea, FTT despite good appetite.
Main chronic lung pathogen: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (S.
aureus early); nasal polyps, male infertility.
Salty baby, hyponatraemic dehydration in heat; ADEK deficiency.
Dx: Newborn screening measures immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) → CFTR panel.
Diagnostic sweat chloride: ≥60 mmol/L (30-59 intermediate); faecal elastase low.
Rx: Airway clearance, dornase alfa (cleaves neutrophil DNA), hypertonic saline, Pseudomonas eradication, azithromycin.
Enzymes every meal, high-calorie diet, ADEK, salt; CFTR modulators (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor).
End-stage: bilateral lung transplant (avoids seeding from native lung); limited by bronchiolitis obliterans.

Def: Asthma = chronic airway inflammation + bronchial hyperresponsiveness + reversible obstruction.
Cause: Atopy (eczema, rhinitis), family history, tobacco smoke, prematurity, obesity.
Triggers: viruses, exercise, allergens, smoke.
Patho: Th2/mast cells → IL-4/5/13, histamine, leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4).
→ bronchospasm (β2-agonist) + oedema (steroid) + mucus → remodelling.
Signs: Recurrent wheeze, night cough, exercise symptoms, chest tightness.
Life-threatening: silent chest, SpO₂ <92%, PEF <33%; normal or rising PaCO2 signals exhaustion.
Dx: Under 5 years: clinical diagnosis (trial of ICS); from 5 years FeNO and spirometry.
FeNO ≥ 35 ppb; reversibility: FEV1 increase of at least 12%; PEF variability.
Rx: Cornerstone controller: inhaled corticosteroid (low dose) → MART/LABA or LTRA → biologics; spacer, action plan.
Acute: oxygen, salbutamol, ipratropium, prednisolone (US: dexamethasone).
Severe acute asthma not responding to nebulised bronchodilators: add IV magnesium sulfate → PICU.

topics.title: Allergy in infants and children. Definition of atopy, atopic diseases.

Def: Atopy is a genetic tendency to produce IgE driven by a Th2 response.
Cause: Atopic march, in order: food allergy - atopic dermatitis -bronchial asthma - allergic rhinitis.
Loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin break the skin barrier; milk, egg, peanut, nuts, fish.
Patho: Th2 (IL-4/13) → IgE on mast cells → cross-linking → histamine, leukotrienes.
IL-5 → eosinophils → late-phase chronic inflammation.
Signs: IgE-mediated (minutes-2 h): urticaria, angioedema, vomiting, wheeze, anaphylaxis.
Non-IgE (hours-days): eczema flare, reflux, proctocolitis, FPIES.
Dx: Food allergy frequency in childhood: parents report approx. 7-10%; in reality 1-2 %.
Allergen specific IgE is not totally reliable; elimination diet, then allergen re-challenge after symptoms disappear.
Rx: Avoidance, dietitian, action plan; milk-allergic infant → extensively hydrolysed formula, not goat's milk.
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 10 µg/kg (0.01 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL), anterolateral thigh; repeat at 5 min.

topics.title: Symptoms and treatment of decompensated heart failure

Def: Heart cannot meet demand → congestion and low output; decompensated = shock/collapse.
Cause: First week: duct-dependent left lesions (HLHS, coarctation), SVT, sepsis.
Large VSD: heart failure at 4-8 weeks because pulmonary vascular resistance falls (AVSD, PDA).
Later: myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, Kawasaki, anaemia.
Patho: ↓ Output → sympathetic + RAAS → tachycardia, sweating, salt/water retention.
↑ Pulmonary venous pressure → tachypnoea; ↑ systemic venous pressure → hepatomegaly.
Signs: Poor feeding with sweating, tachypnoea and failure to thrive.
Most reliable sign of heart failure in an infant: hepatomegaly; gallop, cardiomegaly, weak pulses.
Dx: Echocardiography defines cause; CXR (cardiomegaly), ECG.
BNP/NT-proBNP, electrolytes, renal function, gas and lactate.
Rx: Sit up, careful O,₂ high-calorie NG feeds (up to 150 kcal/kg/day).
Furosemide + spironolactone (spares potassium, blocks aldosterone), ACE inhibitor; milrinone if decompensated.
First-week duct-dependent lesion → prostaglandin E1; then repair defect or transplant.

Def: Congenital heart lesions causing central cyanosis - the 5 Ts.
Cause: R→L shunt, low pulmonary flow: Fallot, pulmonary/tricuspid atresia, critical PS.
Commonest cyanotic lesion in first days: transposition of the great arteries; truncus (22q11), TAPVR.
Patho: Cyanosis visible at ~3-5 g/dL deoxygenated haemoglobin.
Fallot: RVOT obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy; spell → more R→L shunt.
Chronic hypoxia → EPO → polycythaemia, clubbing; brain abscess.
Signs: Fallot: murmur softens in a tet spell; boot-shaped heart.
TGA: profound cyanosis first hours-days, often no murmur; egg on a string.
Dx: Hyperoxia test: PaO2 does not rise with 100% oxygen in cardiac cyanosis.
Echocardiography; pulse-oximetry screening (right hand + foot) detects critical CHD.
Rx: Blue newborn not improving on O₂ → PGE1 (watch apnoea).
Tet spell: knee-chest (raises SVR), O₂, morphine, fluids, propranolol, phenylephrine; repair 3-6 mo.
TGA: prostaglandin → balloon atrial septostomy → arterial switch in first 2-3 weeks.

Def: Congenital heart disease without cyanosis: left-to-right shunts or obstructive lesions.
Cause: Commonest defect: VSD; also ASD, AVSD (Down), PDA (preterm).
Obstruction: coarctation (Turner), aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis (Noonan).
Patho: Long-standing left-to-right shunt reverses = Eisenmenger syndrome.
A small VSD gives a louder murmur: high pressure gradient.
Signs: 4 signs: heart murmur, heart failure, cyanosis, peripheral pulse abnormalities.
Fixed wide splitting of S2 = ASD; PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses.
Coarctation: upper-limb hypertension, weak, delayed femoral pulses.
Dx: Congenital defects are diagnosed with echocardiography.
Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border = VSD.
Innocent murmur: soft, systolic, postural, no other signs.
Rx: Large VSD: surgery in first months; ASD: catheter device at 3-5 years.
Critical coarctation: prostaglandin E1; preterm PDA: ibuprofen, indomethacin or paracetamol.

Def: Heart muscle disease: dilated (commonest), hypertrophic, restrictive.
Cause: DCM: viral myocarditis, anthracycline (doxorubicin) chemotherapy, Duchenne.
HCM: autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutation; newborn: infant of a diabetic mother.
Patho: DCM: can't empty → low EF → dilation → systolic failure, arrhythmia, thrombi.
HCM: can't fill → dynamic LVOT obstruction → sudden death.
RCM: can't stretch → huge atria, early pulmonary hypertension.
Signs: DCM: tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, hepatomegaly, gallop, cool peripheries.
HCM: exertional syncope/dyspnoea; murmur increases with Valsalva and standing.
Dx: Echo: dilated low-EF LV or hypertrophy; also ECG, CXR, troponin, BNP, cardiac MRI.
Screen first-degree relatives.
Rx: DCM: ACE-i, ARB, β -blockers (carvedilol), spironolactone improve survival; transplant if end-stage.
HCM: beta-blockers; avoid inotropes, vasodilators, excess diuretics; high-risk: ICD.
RCM → early transplant.

Def: Myocarditis: heart muscle inflammation; pericarditis: inflamed pericardium ± effusion.
Cause: Commonest cause of myocarditis in children: viral infection (enteroviruses, adenovirus, parvovirus B19).
Pericarditis: viral, purulent (Staphylococcus aureus), TB, autoimmune, post-pericardiotomy.
Patho: Viral + immune myocyte loss → ↓ stroke volume → tachycardia, congestion, arrhythmias.
Tamponade: fluid → ventricles cannot fill → stroke volume falls.
Signs: Myocarditis: tachycardia out of proportion to fever; hepatomegaly = reliable sign of venous congestion.
Pericarditis: pain relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, friction rub.
Tamponade: Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure over 10 mmHg).
Dx: Myocarditis: sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS; troponin, BNP, echo, cardiac MRI.
Pericarditis: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression; echo shows effusion.
Rx: Myocarditis: small fluid boluses, furosemide, inotropes, ECMO; no competitive sport for 3-6 months.
Pericarditis: NSAID + colchicine; tamponade → urgent pericardiocentesis.
Purulent: surgical drainage + IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

topics.title: Infective endocarditis - risk factors, prophylaxis, management

Def: Infection of the endocardium, usually on a valve or defect.
Cause: Risk: CHD with prosthetic material, prosthetic valves, previous IE.
Neonates with normal hearts: central venous catheters.
Viridans streptococci: subacute, after dental bacteraemia; S.
aureus: acute.
Patho: Turbulent jet damages endothelium → platelet-fibrin vegetation → seeded by bacteraemia.
Emboli; immune complexes → glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots.
Signs: Prolonged fever, malaise, new/changing murmur, splenomegaly (FROM JANE).
Painful finger-pulp nodules are Osler nodes; painless palmar macules are Janeway lesions.
Dx: Basis of diagnosis: haemoculture and echocardiography.
Before antibiotics take at least three blood cultures from separate venepunctures.
Rx: IV bactericidal antibiotics for 4-6 weeks: amoxicillin + flucloxacillin [nafcillin] + gentamicin.
Prosthetic material → vancomycin + gentamicin; surgery for heart failure, emboli.
Prophylaxis, high-risk: single oral dose of amoxicillin 30-60 minutes before dental work.

Def: Maldigestion (no enzymes) vs mucosal malabsorption.
Coeliac: permanent immune enteropathy triggered by gluten.
Cause: Maldigestion: cystic fibrosis (commonest cause of pancreatic insufficiency in children).
Mucosal: coeliac, cow's milk allergy, Giardia, Crohn, lactase deficiency.
Coeliac needs HLA-DQ2/DQ8; at risk: T1DM, Down, Turner, IgA deficiency.
Patho: Gliadin → immune villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis → malabsorption; fat loss drags ADEK.
Signs: Classical 6 m-2 y: diarrhoea, distension, wasted buttocks, FTT.
Extraintestinal: hepatitis, osteoporosis, arthritis, isolated iron deficiency, dermatitis herpetiformis.
Dx: First-line: anti-tTG IgA plus total IgA, on a gluten-containing diet.
IgA at least 0.2 g/l to read tTG and EMA reliably.
Avoid biopsy: positive symptoms, tTG AND EMA, positive HLA-DQ2/DQ8.
Rx: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet; antibodies monitor adherence.
CMPA → extensively hydrolysed formula; amino-acid formula if severe.

topics.title: Diseases of oral cavity. Diseases of the oesophagus.

Def: Mouth: mostly infections; oesophagus: reflux, EoE, achalasia, TEF, foreign bodies.
Cause: HSV-1 gingivostomatitis, coxsackie A herpangina, Candida thrush (persistent: immunodeficiency).
TEF: VACTERL association; commonest type is atresia with distal fistula (85%).
Patho: Atopy → eosinophilic oesophagitis → rings, strictures → food impaction.
Button battery burns through the oesophageal wall in 2 hours.
Signs: Gingivostomatitis: swollen bleeding gums, anterior ulcers; herpangina: soft palate only.
Physiological reflux resolves by 12-18 months.
TEF: coughing, choking, cyanosis; achalasia: dysphagia, regurgitation.
Dx: EoE biopsy: at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field.
Achalasia: bird's-beak on barium, absent peristalsis on manometry.
TEF: NG tube coiling on X-ray; pure atresia: gasless abdomen.
Rx: Gingivostomatitis: fluids, analgesia, aciclovir within 72 h.
Severe reflux: fundoplication; achalasia: Heller myotomy.
TEF: surgery, look for VACTERL; swallowed coin: emergency endoscopy (within 2 hours).

Def: Chronic loss of hepatic clearance, synthesis and flow in children.
Cause: Commonest cause of chronic liver failure in children: biliary atresia.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin, Alagille; Wilson (AR, ATP7B), autoimmune hepatitis, hepatitis B/C.
Patho: Can't clear (jaundice, itch), can't build (INR, albumin), can't flow (portal hypertension).
Wilson: copper can't reach bile → liver, basal ganglia, cornea, haemolysis.
Signs: Jaundice, pale stools, pruritus, bruising, ascites, splenomegaly, varices, ADEK deficiency.
Wilson symptoms start after 4-5 years of age.
Dx: INR not correcting with IV vitamin K = synthetic liver failure.
Wilson: serum caeruloplasmin low, 24-hour urinary copper high, KF rings, ATP7B genetics.
Acute liver failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis suggests Wilson disease.
Rx: Cholestatic children: MCT formula + ADEK; ursodeoxycholic acid, cholestyramine for itch.
Spironolactone, lactulose, band ligation; rifaximin lowers ammoniagenic bacteria.
Wilson: penicillamine/trientine, then zinc; end-stage: liver transplantation.

topics.title: Biliary atresia. Liver transplantation in children.

Def: Progressive fibro-obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts in infancy.
Cause: Probably perinatal viral/immune trigger; isolated, or with polysplenia/situs anomalies, cystic.
Patho: Blocked ducts → conjugated bilirubin refluxes → jaundice, dark urine; no stercobilin → acholic stool.
Retained bile → fibrosis → cirrhosis, portal hypertension; no bile → vitamin K bleeding.
Signs: Typical stool feature: clay-coloured (acholic) stool, dark urine.
Term infant jaundiced beyond 2 weeks; thriving, so missed as breast-milk jaundice.
Dx: Jaundice beyond 2 weeks needs a conjugated (split) bilirubin; raised GGT, INR.
Ultrasound: triangular cord sign, small or absent gallbladder; definitive: intraoperative cholangiogram.
Diagnose earlier, but no later than 6 weeks of infancy.
Rx: Kasai portoenterostomy ASAP; ursodiol, prophylactic antibiotics, ADEK, MCT formula.
Fever and returning jaundice = ascending cholangitis → IV antibiotics.
Most common cause of liver transplantation in children; tacrolimus.

topics.title: Inflammatory bowel disease. Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis in childhood

Def: Crohn: transmural with skip lesions; UC: continuous from the rectum.
Cause: Chronic immune-mediated gut inflammation (IBD) of childhood.
Patho: Crohn: transmural, non-caseating granulomas → strictures, fistulae, perianal disease.
UC: mucosal only, crypt abscesses → bloody diarrhoea; linked to PSC.
Signs: Crohn: weight loss; often presents first with growth failure and delayed puberty.
Perianal fissures: not in the midline, deep, not painful.
UC: bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus; high GGT → think sclerosing cholangitis.
Dx: Bloods, stool culture; faecal calprotectin gatekeeps endoscopy.
Ileocolonoscopy + upper endoscopy with biopsies + MR enterography.
Rx: Crohn: first choice exclusive enteral nutrition 6-8 wk, then thiopurine/methotrexate, anti-TNF.
UC: 5-ASA (mesalamine) → steroids → thiopurine/anti-TNF; colectomy curative.
PUCAI ≥65: IV steroids; days 3/5 → infliximab or ciclosporin.

Def: Acute pancreatic inflammation with autodigestion, may progress to SIRS.
Cause: Biliary, trauma (handlebar, NAI), drugs: valproate, azathioprine, L-asparaginase.
Infection (mumps), HUS, HSP, metabolic; recurrent → genetic testing: PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR.
Patho: Premature intra-acinar activation of trypsinogen → autodigestion → cytokines → SIRS, capillary leak.
Fat saponification binds calcium → hypocalcaemia.
Signs: Epigastric pain radiating to back, eased by leaning forward; vomiting, fever.
Tachycardia, ileus; rarely Grey Turner or Cullen sign.
Dx: INSPPIRE needs 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥ 3× ULN, imaging.
Ultrasound first; check calcium, glucose, triglycerides, LFTs.
Rx: Fluids ~1.5-2× maintenance, analgesia incl. opioids; enteral feeding within 48-72 hours.
No routine antibiotics - only infected necrosis or cholangitis.
Treat cause: stop drug, cholecystectomy same admission; pseudocyst forms after more than 4 weeks.

Def: Congenital cleft from failed fusion of facial processes; ~1 in 700 births.
Cause: Maternal smoking, alcohol, phenytoin/valproate, folate deficiency.
Isolated cleft palate is commoner in girls and more often syndromic, e.g. 22q11 deletion.
Patho: Cleft lip: failed fusion of the medial nasal process with the maxillary process.
Palatal shelves fail → no suction seal, VPI.
Tensor veli palatini dysfunction → Eustachian tube can't open → otitis media with effusion.
Signs: Feeding difficulty, nasal milk reflux; glue ear.
Hypernasal speech (VPI); Pierre Robin: micrognathia, glossoptosis, U-shaped cleft palate.
Dx: Often seen at 20-week anomaly scan (lip more than palate).
Any cleft palate → hearing test; syndromic features → 22q11 testing.
Rx: Cleft team; squeezable bottles, upright feeding, weight monitoring.
Lip repaired at about 3 months; soft palate closed at 1 year, before first words.
Grommets, speech therapy, alveolar bone graft 8-11 years.

Def: Ileus: bowel obstruction, mechanical (lumen blocked) or paralytic (peristalsis stops).
Cause: Mechanical: adhesions, incarcerated hernia, intussusception, volvulus, atresia.
Paralytic: post-surgery, sepsis, peritonitis, hypokalaemia, opioids, vincristine.
Intussusception: usual lead point Peyer's patches; over 3 y: Meckel's, polyp, lymphoma.
Patho: Mechanical → tinkling bowel sounds; paralytic → silent, distended abdomen.
Colicky pain turning constant suggests strangulation: ischaemia, fever, rising lactate.
Ileocolic intussusception → mucosal ischaemia → redcurrant-jelly stool (late).
Signs: Intussusception 3 months - 3 years: paroxysmal colic, pallor, legs drawn up, lethargy.
Sausage mass (RUQ); vomiting, later bilious.
Dx: Ultrasound: target (doughnut) sign.
Commonest cause of strangulation ileus in children: incarcerated hernia.
Suspected SBO: unstable → X-ray; stable → CT with IV contrast.
Rx: Obstruction: drip and suck, analgesia, surgical review; complete SBO: laparotomy.
Intussusception: resuscitate → air (pneumatic) enema reduction; ~10% recur.
Surgery: strangulation, peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed reduction.

topics.title: Diseases of the colon. Obstipation Hirschsprung disease.

Def: About 95% of childhood constipation is functional; Hirschsprung = congenital aganglionosis.
Cause: Functional: weaning, toilet training, school, anal fissure (tight sphincter → mucosal tear).
Hirschsprung: failed neural crest migration; Down syndrome association.
Patho: Withholding → harder stool → pain → dilated rectum → overflow soiling (liquid stool around impacted faeces).
Aganglionic rectum can't relax → functional obstruction.
Signs: Functional: withholding postures, packed rectum, soiling; infantile dyschezia: infant strains ~10 minutes.
Hirschsprung: meconium delayed beyond 48 hours, distension, bilious vomiting.
Rectum empty with explosive release on withdrawal.
Dx: Rectal suction biopsy: absent ganglion cells, raised acetylcholinesterase.
Contrast enema: transition zone; manometry: absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex.
Anal fissure: physical exam (DRE, anoscopy).
Rx: Functional: disimpaction with macrogol, then maintenance for months, not days; toileting.
Hirschsprung: rectal washouts → pull-through operation.
Feared complication: enterocolitis - fever, distension, explosive foul diarrhoea.

Def: Acute inflammation of the appendix from luminal obstruction.
Cause: Obstruction of the lumen by a faecolith (older) or lymphoid hyperplasia (younger, after viral illness).
Patho: Obstruction → pressure, venous failure, bacterial invasion → gangrene → perforation after 36-48 hours.
Visceral T10 → periumbilical pain → parietal peritoneum → localised RIF pain.
